distractorExplanations.a: Mutual aid shares resources; it does not hand incident command to another facility—the host site and fire department keep command roles.
distractorExplanations.c: Mutual aid is an emergency response arrangement; it has nothing to do with meeting the PSM process hazard analysis element.
distractorExplanations.d: Mutual aid supplements, not substitutes for, each site's own response capability for initial and credible incidents.

options.a: Storage, handling, and use of flammable and combustible liquids in tanks and containers
options.b: Prevention of fire and dust explosions from handling combustible particulate solids
options.c: Fire safety for storage, use, and handling of hazardous materials in all occupancies
options.d: Storage, handling, and use of LP-Gas containers, piping, and dispensing systems

distractorExplanations.a: That is the scope of NFPA 30; NFPA 400 covers other classified hazardous materials such as oxidizers, corrosives and toxics.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes the NFPA 652/654 combustible dust standards, not the NFPA 400 Hazardous Materials Code.
distractorExplanations.d: LP-Gas systems are governed by NFPA 58, the Liquefied Petroleum Gas Code, rather than by NFPA 400.

options.a: Packaging type and container size, such as drums, totes, or gas cylinders, rather than chemistry
options.b: DOT shipping hazard class placards assigned to the material for highway transport
options.c: NFPA 13 commodity classes I through IV and Group A, B, and C plastics designations
options.d: Hazard categories such as flammable, oxidizing, corrosive, and water-reactive characteristics

distractorExplanations.a: Container type affects allowable quantities, but classification itself rests on the material's physical and health hazards.
distractorExplanations.b: DOT transport classes differ from the NFPA 400 / fire code hazard categories used to set storage and use limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Commodity classes are NFPA 13 sprinkler design categories for ordinary storage, not hazardous materials classifications.

options.a: Quantity limits per control area, fire-resistance ratings, ventilation, and automatic sprinkler requirements
options.b: Labeling and SDS availability, with no quantity cap per control area once containers are properly labeled and dated
options.c: Container color coding and shelf height, with sprinklers omitted when stored below eye level
options.d: Exit enclosure placement for responder access, provided containers are in safety cans

distractorExplanations.b: Labeling is a HazCom requirement; it does not lift the maximum allowable quantities per control area.
distractorExplanations.c: Sprinkler requirements depend on liquid class, quantity and storage arrangement, not on shelf height relative to eye level.
distractorExplanations.d: Flammable liquids may not be stored in exit enclosures; safety cans do not make egress paths acceptable storage.

options.a: Commingling allowed if both remain sealed in original manufacturer shipping containers
options.b: Separation by distance, barriers, or separate rooms per compatibility requirements
options.c: Storage on a shared spill containment pallet sized for the largest single container
options.d: Alphabetical shelving with SDS binders posted at the storage room entrance door

distractorExplanations.a: Original containers can fail in a fire and let materials react; incompatibles still need distance, barriers or separate rooms.
distractorExplanations.c: A shared containment sump lets incompatible spills mix; separate containment or segregation is required for incompatibles.
distractorExplanations.d: Alphabetical arrangement ignores reactivity; posting SDS informs staff but does not separate oxidizers from flammables.

options.a: Placement beside combustible pallets and wood fences, since open outdoor air quickly disperses any oxidizer decomposition gases
options.b: Drainage that collects runoff into a shared pit with flammable liquid spills, plus a tarp cover for weather
options.c: Separation from combustible construction, drainage to avoid contaminating other materials, and exposure to weather controls
options.d: Storage directly on asphalt paving with no spacing between stacks, relying on sprinklers at nearby buildings

distractorExplanations.a: Oxidizers intensify combustion of nearby fuels; outdoor storage needs separation from combustibles, not adjacency to them.
distractorExplanations.b: Combining oxidizer runoff with flammable spills creates a reactive mixture; drainage must keep incompatible materials apart.
distractorExplanations.d: Asphalt is combustible and building sprinklers do not protect yard storage; oxidizers need noncombustible surfaces and spacing.

options.a: Display and sale of merchandise to the public with frequent customer turnover
options.b: Storage of goods, merchandise, or vehicles with few occupants present
options.c: Transaction of business such as offices with incidental equipment use
options.d: Operations involving fabrication, assembly, or processing of materials

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a mercantile occupancy under NFPA 101, not an industrial occupancy where products are made or processed.
distractorExplanations.b: That is a storage occupancy; industrial occupancies are defined by manufacturing, processing, assembly or repair operations.
distractorExplanations.c: Office and professional work is a business occupancy under NFPA 101, not industrial even when some equipment is used.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Industrial occupancies include factories and workshops where production equipment and materials create specific egress and protection requirements. Their occupant loads and hazards are distinct from mercantile or storage uses.

options.a: Building area or fire load exceeds thresholds in NFPA 101 for that occupancy subclass
options.b: The building has fewer than two exits serving each floor of the production and assembly area
options.c: Employees are trained in portable fire extinguisher use under OSHA 1910.157
options.d: The structure is Type I or Type II noncombustible construction of any size

distractorExplanations.b: Exit count is a means-of-egress requirement; deficient exits are corrected by egress design, not by triggering sprinklers.
distractorExplanations.c: Extinguisher training is an OSHA workforce requirement and has no effect on whether automatic sprinklers are mandated.
distractorExplanations.d: Noncombustible construction does not remove sprinkler triggers; contents, area and hazard still drive sprinkler mandates.

options.a: NFPA 30 flammable liquid storage limits for the control areas they occupy
options.b: NFPA 72 detection spacing alone, since early alarm is what controls dust explosions
options.c: NFPA 652 dust hazard analysis and applicable NFPA commodity/process standards
options.d: NFPA 101 egress travel distances and nothing beyond the occupancy chapter

distractorExplanations.a: NFPA 30 governs flammable liquids; combustible dust operations need the NFPA 652 DHA and the commodity-specific dust standards.
distractorExplanations.b: Detection gives warning but cannot prevent or vent a deflagration; dust hazards require the NFPA 652 DHA and mitigation.
distractorExplanations.d: Life safety egress rules alone do not address dust containment, ignition control, housekeeping or explosion protection.

options.a: Hot work operations such as welding and cutting in occupied, completed buildings
options.b: Fire protection features of completed buildings during their occupied life
options.c: Inspection, testing, and maintenance of water-based fire protection systems in existing buildings
options.d: Fire safety during construction, alteration, and demolition of buildings and structures

distractorExplanations.a: Hot work in general is NFPA 51B; NFPA 241 addresses fire safety for the whole construction, alteration or demolition project.
distractorExplanations.b: Ongoing life safety in occupied buildings is NFPA 101 and the fire code; NFPA 241 covers safeguards during construction work.
distractorExplanations.c: That is NFPA 25; NFPA 241 addresses water-based protection only as part of the construction-phase fire safety program.

options.a: Implementing and enforcing the site fire safety plan, permits, and coordination
options.b: Designing the permanent sprinkler and fire alarm systems for the completed building
options.c: Issuing the certificate of occupancy once the building fire systems are accepted
options.d: Conducting the final acceptance tests of standpipes and sprinklers for the AHJ

distractorExplanations.b: Permanent system design is the fire protection engineer's role; the FPPM manages fire prevention on the active site.
distractorExplanations.c: The AHJ issues the certificate of occupancy; the FPPM is the owner-designated manager of the construction fire prevention program.
distractorExplanations.d: Acceptance testing is performed by installing contractors and witnessed by the AHJ; it is not an FPPM duty under NFPA 241.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: The FPPM administers hot work, housekeeping, standpipe readiness, and liaison with AHJ on the construction site. These duties apply during construction.

options.a: Installed only after the building is fully enclosed and the permanent fire pump has been accepted
options.b: Available and maintained as construction progresses in accordance with NFPA 241 staged requirements
options.c: Kept dry and disconnected until the final AHJ acceptance test so that freezing cannot damage the piping
options.d: Extended to within four floors below the highest working deck as the building rises

distractorExplanations.a: NFPA 241 requires standpipes to follow construction upward, not wait for building enclosure or fire pump acceptance.
distractorExplanations.c: Disconnected standpipes give firefighters no water during construction fires; freeze risk is handled with dry systems, not removal.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 241 requires the standpipe within one floor of the highest secured decking, not four floors below the work level.

options.a: Stockpiling spare plywood on scaffold decks so workers do not haul materials up daily
options.b: Treating formwork with a fire-retardant coating so debris may accumulate until the project ends
options.c: Limiting accumulation, prohibiting unnecessary storage on scaffolds, and expediting removal
options.d: Covering scrap formwork with tarps overnight and removing it at the monthly site cleanup

distractorExplanations.a: Stockpiled plywood on scaffolds adds fuel at height and is exactly the unnecessary storage NFPA 241 housekeeping limits.
distractorExplanations.b: Retardant coatings slow ignition but do not justify letting combustible debris accumulate; removal remains the primary control.
distractorExplanations.d: Tarps add fuel and monthly cleanups allow buildup; NFPA 241 expects prompt, routine removal of combustible waste.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Construction debris and combustible materials increase fire load; NFPA 241 emphasizes housekeeping and controlled storage. Removal should happen as soon as materials are no longer needed.

options.a: A permit only when hot work occurs within 10 ft of exposed combustible materials
options.b: Verbal approval from the subcontractor foreman, with a fire watch for large jobs
options.c: A daily safety meeting sign-in in place of individual hot work permits
options.d: Permits, area preparation, fire watch, and coordination with the FPPM

distractorExplanations.a: NFPA 51B uses a 35 ft (11 m) radius for combustibles; a 10 ft threshold would leave nearby fuels unprotected.
distractorExplanations.b: Hot work needs a written permit from the permit authorizing individual; a foreman's verbal okay does not satisfy NFPA 241.
distractorExplanations.c: A toolbox talk does not replace per-job permits that verify area preparation, extinguishers and fire watch assignment.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Construction hot work follows permit programs paralleling NFPA 51B concepts under the site-specific NFPA 241 plan. Applicable AHJ provisions also apply.

options.a: Outdoors or in approved locations with separation from exposures per NFPA 58
options.b: Adjacent to building exits so delivery hoses and piping runs stay as short as possible
options.c: Inside ventilated mechanical rooms of the building to protect them from vehicle impact
options.d: In below-grade pits or basements so vapors stay contained near the container

distractorExplanations.b: Placing LP-Gas vessels at exits exposes egress paths to a leak or fire; NFPA 58 sets separation from buildings and openings.
distractorExplanations.c: NFPA 58 generally locates LP-Gas storage containers outdoors; indoor placement is limited to specific small-cylinder cases.
distractorExplanations.d: LP-Gas vapor is heavier than air and collects in pits and basements, creating flammable pockets rather than safe containment.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: NFPA 58 specifies separation distances from buildings, property lines, and ignition sources for LPG containers and systems. Site AHJ requirements also apply.

options.a: Relieve pressure into the liquid outlet line so product can be delivered at a higher rate
options.b: Discharge vapor if internal pressure exceeds safe limits due to heat exposure or overfilling
options.c: Close tightly and stay closed once a pressure rise is sensed, sealing the container contents
options.d: Allow reduced separation distances to buildings, since venting prevents container rupture

distractorExplanations.a: Relief valves vent to atmosphere for overpressure protection; they do not feed product into delivery lines.
distractorExplanations.c: That confuses relief valves with shutoff or excess-flow valves; a relief valve opens to vent, it does not seal on pressure rise.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 58 separation distances apply independently; relief valves do not permit closer siting to buildings.

options.a: Extinguish the venting relief-valve flame first, then begin applying cooling water to the shell
options.b: Apply water to the vapor space only after the relief valve has stopped venting and pressure drops
options.c: Cool exposed containers with water streams from a safe distance while preventing BLEVE conditions
options.d: Direct hose streams at the liquid-wetted shell, since the vapor space is cooled by the venting

distractorExplanations.a: Extinguishing the vent flame lets unburned gas accumulate and reignite; cooling the shell is the priority, not flame knockdown.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for venting to stop wastes critical time; cooling must start promptly, especially where flame impinges on the vapor space.
distractorExplanations.d: The vapor space has no liquid to absorb heat, so it weakens fastest; flame impingement there is the classic BLEVE precursor.

options.a: Place gas detectors near the ceiling, since LP-Gas vapor rises once it leaves the container
options.b: Assume vapor disperses within a few feet, so drains and pits need no evaluation
options.c: Rely on roof ridge vents to clear leaks from buildings near the storage area
options.d: Account for accumulation in low areas, trenches, and basements near the storage and piping

distractorExplanations.a: That fits lighter-than-air gases such as natural gas; LP-Gas vapor is about 1.5 to 2 times heavier than air and sinks.
distractorExplanations.b: Heavier-than-air LP-Gas vapor can travel along grade and pool in drains and pits far from the leak source.
distractorExplanations.c: Roof-level vents clear lighter gases; LP-Gas leaks require low-level ventilation and attention to floor-level traps.

options.a: Upright securing, protection from vehicle impact, separation from oxidizers, and ventilation
options.b: Horizontal stacking of cylinders in exit corridors to keep them close to points of use
options.c: Storage inside closed vehicles or vans overnight to protect cylinders from theft
options.d: Placement against the building wall beside the fire department connections for quick, easy access

distractorExplanations.b: LP-Gas cylinders must be stored upright with relief valves in the vapor space and must not be stored in or near exits.
distractorExplanations.c: Enclosed vehicles trap leaking heavier-than-air vapor and heat, creating ignition and overpressure risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Cylinders near FDCs obstruct fire department access and expose the building; NFPA 58 requires separation from openings.

options.a: Steel rack uprights are left unpainted, and storage remains below the sprinkler design height and commodity class limits
options.b: Commodity classification is underestimated and aisle widths or sprinkler design do not match actual storage height
options.c: Aisles are widened from 8 ft to 10 ft while commodity class and storage height stay within the sprinkler design
options.d: Storage height is lowered below the design height while the commodity classification matches the tested criteria

distractorExplanations.a: Unpainted steel does not change fire behavior, and storage within design height and class keeps the sprinkler design valid.
distractorExplanations.c: Wider aisles reduce fire jump between racks; with class and height unchanged, the sprinkler design remains adequate.
distractorExplanations.d: Storage lower than designed with correct classification reduces the challenge to sprinklers rather than increasing risk.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Misclassified commodities or changed storage arrays can exceed sprinkler design limits, leading to uncontrolled fire spread. Storage arrangement changes have the same effect.

options.a: Pre-wet the top tier of storage so ceiling sprinklers can operate at a lower design density
options.b: Replace ceiling sprinklers in racks over 12 ft high so a single in-rack system protects the whole building
options.c: Control or suppress fire within the rack structure where ceiling sprinklers alone may not penetrate
options.d: Provide exposure protection for building walls and columns adjacent to the storage racks

distractorExplanations.a: In-rack heads open on heat at their own level inside the rack; they are not a pre-wetting system for reducing ceiling density.
distractorExplanations.b: In-rack sprinklers usually supplement ceiling protection; NFPA 13 rack designs combine both rather than omitting the ceiling system.
distractorExplanations.d: Column and wall protection is a separate steel-protection concept; in-rack heads target fire inside rack flues and voids.

options.a: Vertical gaps between side-by-side loads, running parallel to the direction of loading across the full rack depth
options.b: Horizontal clearances between the top of storage and the sprinkler deflectors at the ceiling
options.c: Aisle spaces between rack rows that provide forklift access and limit fire jump between racks
options.d: Vertical openings along the row length between loads that allow heat venting and sprinkler water penetration

distractorExplanations.a: That defines a transverse flue; the longitudinal flue runs along the row length between back-to-back loads.
distractorExplanations.b: That is the clearance to ceiling sprinklers (typically 18 in. minimum), not a flue space within the rack structure.
distractorExplanations.c: Aisles separate rack rows; flue spaces are the narrower vertical openings inside the rack between loads.

options.a: Keep the process running at reduced rate by adjusting setpoints when parameters drift
options.b: Automatically move the process to a safe state when critical parameters exceed defined limits
options.c: Alert operators so they can decide on a manual response, with no final element action of its own
options.d: Replace mechanical integrity testing, since a SIL-rated system needs no proof testing

distractorExplanations.a: Setpoint adjustment is the basic process control system's job; an SIS acts independently to reach a safe state.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes an alarm layer; an SIS or interlock acts on final elements such as valves without waiting for operators.
distractorExplanations.d: SIS functions require periodic proof testing under IEC 61511 / ISA 84; the SIL claim depends on that testing being done.

options.a: Vacuum collapse when the vessel is drained or cooled with vents closed
options.b: Toxic vapor release to the surrounding work area during normal, steady-state operation
options.c: Overpressure from runaway reactions, blocked outlets, or external fire exposure
options.d: Flame propagation back into the reactor through open vent piping

distractorExplanations.a: Vacuum collapse is addressed by vacuum breakers or vacuum relief, not by the reactor's overpressure relief system.
distractorExplanations.b: Relief systems act during upsets and may themselves release material; they do not prevent toxic exposure in normal operation.
distractorExplanations.d: Preventing flashback through vent lines is the job of flame arresters, not pressure relief devices.

options.a: Located inside the process unit right next to the equipment so operators can close them by hand
options.b: Locked in the open position between turnarounds to prevent accidental closure upsets
options.c: Tested only during plant turnarounds every five years to avoid production upsets
options.d: Accessible, clearly identified, tested per procedure, and positioned to stop hazardous flow

distractorExplanations.a: Manual valves inside the unit may be unreachable during a fire or release; EIVs are placed or actuated from a safe location.
distractorExplanations.b: Locking EIVs open defeats their emergency function; they must remain operable and be function-tested.
distractorExplanations.c: Five-year turnaround-only testing is too infrequent; partial-stroke or periodic tests per procedure verify reliability.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Isolation valves enable rapid source control during leaks; concealment or welding defeats emergency use. Placement is based on credible release scenarios.

options.a: Quantify whether independent protection layers reduce risk to tolerable levels
options.b: Identify process deviations node by node using guide words such as no, more, and less
options.c: Calculate dispersion and overpressure distances for siting occupied buildings
options.d: Rank each component failure mode by severity, occurrence, and detection scores

distractorExplanations.b: Guide-word deviation finding is HAZOP; LOPA takes scenarios identified by a PHA and checks protection-layer adequacy.
distractorExplanations.c: Consequence modeling for building siting (API 752/753) is separate from LOPA's frequency-based layer assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Severity-occurrence-detection ranking is FMEA's risk priority number, not LOPA's order-of-magnitude analysis of IPLs.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: LOPA evaluates initiating events, consequences, and IPL effectiveness with order-of-magnitude risk estimates. It is applied to specific scenarios.

options.a: An identical replacement part from the same manufacturer specification is installed
options.b: A change affects process chemicals, technology, equipment, or procedures beyond replacement-in-kind
options.c: A temporary change lasting less than 30 days is made to the operating procedures for a covered process
options.d: The plant's production rate increases within the existing safe operating limits

distractorExplanations.c: OSHA PSM applies MOC to temporary changes too; a short duration does not exempt a procedure change from review.
distractorExplanations.d: Running within the documented safe operating limits is not a change; MOC is triggered when the limits themselves change.
distractorExplanations.a: Parking lot paving unrelated to process does not trigger MOC.

options.a: Whether the change pays back its cost within the budget year and already has a signed capital authorization
options.b: Whether the original PHA team members are available to sign off on the change form
options.c: What could go wrong, what safeguards are needed, who must be trained, and what documents require updating
options.d: Whether the change can start immediately and be documented after the next turnaround

distractorExplanations.a: Cost justification is a business decision; MOC review must address safety impact, safeguards, training and documentation.
distractorExplanations.b: Signatures are administrative; MOC must evaluate the safety impact and the required safeguards, training and document updates.
distractorExplanations.d: MOC requires review and authorization before implementation; documenting after the fact defeats its purpose.

options.a: A shift supervisor's verbal approval, since the bypass is temporary and attended
options.b: A work order only, because interlock bypasses under 72 hours are treated as replacement-in-kind
options.c: A PSSR after the trial ends, documenting the bypass once the interlock is restored
options.d: Formal MOC authorization with hazard analysis, duration limits, and restoration verification

distractorExplanations.a: Temporary changes are covered by MOC; a verbal approval skips hazard review, time limits and restoration checks.
distractorExplanations.b: Bypassing an interlock is not replacement-in-kind, and PSM has no 72-hour exemption for temporary changes.
distractorExplanations.c: PSSR verifies readiness before startup of a change; it does not replace prior MOC authorization of the bypass.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Even temporary changes affecting safeguards need documented review and controlled restoration. Formal approval is part of that authorization.

options.a: The change is documented, operators trained, and P&IDs and procedures updated
options.b: Operators are briefed on the new safeguard at the next annual refresher training session
options.c: The PHA recommendation is marked closed once the purchase order for the safeguard is issued
options.d: P&IDs are updated at the next five-year PHA revalidation rather than at installation

distractorExplanations.b: Training must precede reliance on the safeguard; waiting for an annual refresher leaves operators unaware at startup.
distractorExplanations.c: A purchase order is not implementation; closure requires installation, training and updated documentation via MOC.
distractorExplanations.d: Process safety information must be current when the change is made, not deferred to the next PHA revalidation.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Closing PHA items through changes ties into MOC—implementation, training, and document control must align. All of this must happen before relying on the safeguard.

options.a: The MOC hazard review has identified the deviations and failure scenarios that the change could introduce
options.b: Construction meets design, safeguards are functional, procedures are ready, and training is complete
options.c: The PHA for the facility has been revalidated within the past five years
options.d: Mechanical integrity inspections are scheduled for the equipment's first turnaround

distractorExplanations.a: Hazard identification happens in the MOC review; PSSR then verifies installation, safeguards and training before startup.
distractorExplanations.c: Five-year PHA revalidation is a separate PSM element; PSSR checks that the specific change is ready to operate.
distractorExplanations.d: Scheduling future inspections is not readiness verification; PSSR confirms equipment and safeguards work before startup.

options.a: Follows the normal step-by-step shutdown procedure, only faster, when operators choose
options.b: Alerts operators to abnormal conditions and waits for them to stop feeds manually
options.c: Rapidly places the process in a safe state in response to abnormal conditions
options.d: Holds the unit at its normal operating point by trimming control valve setpoints

distractorExplanations.a: ESD bypasses normal sequencing and acts on abnormal conditions; it is not an accelerated, operator-chosen normal shutdown.
distractorExplanations.b: That is an alarm function; an ESD system acts on final elements itself to isolate and depressurize the process.
distractorExplanations.d: Setpoint trimming is basic process control; ESD overrides normal control to reach a safe state.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: ESD prioritizes hazard mitigation—stopping feeds, isolating equipment, venting pressure—over production continuity. It acts without normal sequencing delays.

options.a: NFPA 30 container storage criteria, since Group A plastics are treated as flammable liquids
options.b: NFPA 13 Class III commodity criteria, since corrugated cartons reduce plastics to an ordinary commodity
options.c: NFPA 25 inspection frequencies, which set the sprinkler density for the plastics storage
options.d: NFPA 13 commodity classification and storage arrangement criteria for uncartoned/cartoned plastics

distractorExplanations.a: Group A plastics are solid commodities classified in NFPA 13; NFPA 30 addresses flammable and combustible liquids.
distractorExplanations.b: Cartoning does not reduce Group A plastics to Class III; cartoned Group A plastics remain a higher-hazard classification.
distractorExplanations.c: NFPA 25 governs inspection, testing and maintenance; design density comes from NFPA 13 commodity and storage criteria.

options.a: Monitoring hot work areas, maintaining extinguishers accessible, and notifying the FPPM
options.b: Issuing hot work permits and signing off area preparation before welding begins
options.c: Performing the welding while watching for sparks, so a separate fire watch person is unneeded
options.d: Leaving the area as soon as hot work stops, since smoldering is unlikely afterward

distractorExplanations.b: Permits are issued by the permit authorizing individual; the fire watch monitors, it does not authorize the work.
distractorExplanations.c: The fire watch must be a separate, dedicated person; the operator focused on the work cannot also serve as fire watch.
distractorExplanations.d: Fire watch continues after work ends because smoldering fires often develop after the hot work has stopped.

cfps-readiness-check-facility-hazard-man.explanation: Fire watch supports the FPPM by observing ignition hazards during and after hot work and maintaining initial attack capability. Unsafe conditions are reported to the FPPM.

options.a: Each program is audited by separate teams so findings from one do not bias the other two programs
options.b: Identified hazards have safeguards, changes are reviewed before implementation, and responders know current risks
options.c: Emergency plans are rewritten at the five-year PHA revalidation, keeping documents synchronized
options.d: PHA recommendations are closed through MOC, while emergency plans keep the original design-basis chemical inventory

distractorExplanations.a: Independent silos are the failure mode; integration means PHA findings feed MOC and emergency plans share current hazard data.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency plans must be updated whenever changes alter hazards, not held until the five-year PHA revalidation.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving the emergency plan on the original inventory means responders face hazards the MOC process already changed.

options.a: Authorize and control temporary ignition-source activities where fire or explosion hazards exist
options.b: Replace fixed fire detection in production areas where welding and cutting occur on a regular basis
options.c: Document welder certification and weld quality for structural and pressure piping work
options.d: Control combustible dust accumulation and housekeeping frequency in process areas

distractorExplanations.b: Permits supplement detection and cover temporary hot work; designated permanent welding areas are handled differently.
distractorExplanations.c: Welder qualification and weld quality are covered by AWS/ASME codes, not by the fire-prevention hot work permit.
distractorExplanations.d: Dust housekeeping falls under NFPA 652/654 programs; the hot work permit controls temporary ignition sources.

options.a: Combustibles within 10 ft (3 m) are removed or covered and a fire extinguisher is nearby
options.b: Combustibles within 35 ft (11 m) are removed, covered, or protected and a fire watch is assigned
options.c: Combustibles within 50 ft (15 m) are removed, and sprinklers over the work area are temporarily shut off
options.d: The welder's PPE is inspected and the hot work is scheduled outside occupied hours

distractorExplanations.a: NFPA 51B uses a 35 ft (11 m) radius; 10 ft is far short of how far sparks and slag can travel.
distractorExplanations.c: Sprinklers must stay in service during hot work; shutting them off removes protection exactly when ignition risk peaks.
distractorExplanations.d: PPE protects the welder and timing does not control ignition; the permit must address combustibles and a fire watch.

options.a: Until the arc stops, since sparks are no longer produced once welding ends
options.b: 15 minutes after work ends, unless an area sprinkler system is in service
options.c: 30 minutes after work ends, or longer if local policy or hazards require
options.d: 24 hours after work ends, with the fire watch remaining on site overnight

distractorExplanations.a: Smoldering fires often develop after hot work stops, so the fire watch must continue beyond the end of welding.
distractorExplanations.b: 15 minutes is too short; the minimum post-work watch is longer, and sprinklers do not shorten it.
distractorExplanations.d: A 24-hour watch is not the minimum; extended fire monitoring beyond the watch is set by hazard, not a fixed day.

options.a: Completion of the planned work scope before the permit's expiration time
options.b: A different qualified welder from the same crew taking over the task
options.c: A normal shift change with a documented face-to-face handover briefing to the next crew
options.d: Change in conditions such as unexpected flammable atmosphere or alarm activation

distractorExplanations.a: Finishing early ends the work while the permit was valid; it is closed out, not invalidated by a hazard change.
distractorExplanations.b: A crew substitution is handled by updating the permit; it is not the condition change that voids authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: A documented handover maintains continuity; permits are voided by changed hazards, not routine shift transfers.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Permits are void when hazards change, preparation is inadequate, or emergency conditions arise; work must stop and be re-evaluated. Incomplete area preparation also voids the permit.

options.a: Removing accumulations of combustibles and maintaining clear egress
options.b: Increasing storage density so fewer square feet of floor hold combustibles
options.c: Keeping oily rags in open bins so they can dry out between uses
options.d: Scheduling waste removal around quarterly fire safety audits

distractorExplanations.b: Denser storage raises fire load per area and can exceed sprinkler design; housekeeping reduces fuel instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Open bins let oily rags self-heat to ignition; they belong in listed self-closing metal containers.
distractorExplanations.d: Quarterly removal lets fuel accumulate for months; housekeeping requires routine, frequent waste removal.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Good housekeeping reduces available fuel, maintains travel paths, and supports other controls like sprinkler effectiveness. It also keeps ignition sources separated from fuel.

options.a: Exceeding the allowable sprinkler storage height in the aisle
options.b: Impaired egress and increased fuel load in occupied paths
options.c: Lack of a hot work permit for the warehouse
options.d: Missing exit signage at the warehouse entrance

distractorExplanations.a: Nothing indicates storage near the ceiling; the finding is about exit aisles blocked with combustible cartons.
distractorExplanations.c: No hot work is described; the deficiency is obstructed exit aisles loaded with cardboard fuel.
distractorExplanations.d: Signs mark exits, but the problem here is that the egress path itself is physically blocked by combustibles.

options.a: Spreading sawdust to absorb the oil and sweeping it up at the end of each month
options.b: Washing drips toward floor drains with water so the floor stays clean between shifts
options.c: Routine cleaning, drip pans, and proper disposal of oil-soaked materials in closed metal containers
options.d: Placing cardboard sheets under the machines and replacing them only once they are fully saturated with oil

distractorExplanations.a: Oil-soaked sawdust is itself fuel and can self-heat; leaving it for a month adds hazard rather than removing it.
distractorExplanations.b: Hosing oil to drains spreads it, creates environmental and vapor problems, and does not stop the source.
distractorExplanations.d: Saturated cardboard is a wick and fuel; drip pans and routine cleanup with metal waste cans control oil properly.

options.a: Test the dust for Kst and Pmax before deciding whether any analysis is needed
options.b: Install explosion venting on every enclosure that contains dust before any analysis is performed
options.c: Write a housekeeping procedure based on the OSHA 1/32-inch dust layer rule
options.d: Conduct a dust hazard analysis (DHA) for processes handling combustible particulate solids

distractorExplanations.a: Explosibility testing supports the DHA but is not the first step; NFPA 652 requires the DHA to determine hazards.
distractorExplanations.b: Mitigation such as venting is selected from DHA findings; installing it first skips hazard identification.
distractorExplanations.c: Housekeeping thresholds follow from the DHA; the 1/32-in. layer guide is a benchmark, not the first NFPA 652 step.

options.a: Deflagration from dust cloud ignition and secondary explosions from accumulated dust on surfaces
options.b: Spontaneous heating of stored wood flour and corrosion of the silo bin's internal steel wall surfaces
options.c: Flammable vapor ignition and boiling liquid expanding vapor explosion of the silo
options.d: Smoldering fire in the dust layer and carbon monoxide exposure at ground level only

distractorExplanations.b: Self-heating matters for some organics, but corrosion is not a fire hazard; the DHA focus is primary and secondary deflagration.
distractorExplanations.c: Vapor ignition and BLEVE apply to flammable liquids and pressurized gases, not to a wood flour particulate silo.
distractorExplanations.d: Smoldering and CO are secondary concerns; the defining dust hazard pair is primary deflagration plus secondary explosions.

options.a: Prevention of fires and dust explosions in grain elevators, flour mills, feed mills, and agricultural facilities
options.b: Prevention of fire and dust explosions in chemical, dye, pharmaceutical, and related processing facilities
options.c: Prevention of fire and dust explosions in wood processing and woodworking facilities
options.d: Prevention of fires and explosions in the production and handling of combustible metals

distractorExplanations.a: Agricultural and food dusts are covered by NFPA 61, a commodity-specific standard, not NFPA 654.
distractorExplanations.c: Wood processing and woodworking dusts fall under NFPA 664, not the general NFPA 654 standard.
distractorExplanations.d: Combustible metals such as aluminum and magnesium are covered by NFPA 484, not NFPA 654.

options.a: Raising duct conveying velocity so that dust cannot settle and a flame front cannot travel back upstream
options.b: Fire dampers rated for 1½ hours at each duct penetration of the dust collector room
options.c: Isolation devices such as explosion vents, chemical suppression, or isolation valves on ductwork
options.d: One common header connecting all collectors so pressure equalizes between units

distractorExplanations.a: Velocity limits dust settling but does not stop flame propagation through ductwork; isolation hardware is required.
distractorExplanations.b: Fire dampers stop fire spread through rated barriers; they cannot react fast enough to isolate a deflagration.
distractorExplanations.d: A shared unprotected header is a path for deflagration propagation between collectors, not a mitigation.

options.a: The lowest temperature at which a dust layer ignites on a hot surface
options.b: The lowest spark energy needed to ignite a dust cloud at its most easily ignited concentration
options.c: The concentration giving the maximum rate of pressure rise, used to calculate Kst
options.d: The lowest concentration in air capable of propagating flame through the dust cloud

distractorExplanations.a: That is the minimum layer ignition temperature (hot surface), not the minimum explosible concentration.
distractorExplanations.b: That defines minimum ignition energy (MIE), a separate dust property measured in millijoules.
distractorExplanations.c: Kst comes from the maximum rate of pressure rise near optimum concentration; MEC is the lower explosible limit.

options.a: Limit vapor release, prevent spills, and reduce ignition likelihood from static or external sources
options.b: Permit storing larger quantities at each workstation, since approved containers lift the fire code quantity limits
options.c: Eliminate bonding and grounding during transfers because safety cans are conductive
options.d: Raise the flash point of the liquid so it is reclassified from Class I to Class II

distractorExplanations.b: Approved containers do not raise quantity limits at workstations; maximum allowable quantities still apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Safety cans still need bonding during transfer; conductivity helps only when a bonding path is actually connected.
distractorExplanations.d: Containers do not change a liquid's flash point or class; classification is a property of the liquid itself.

options.a: Left vented open so vapor pressure inside the containers can equalize
options.b: Closed tightly and limited to the quantity and arrangement permitted by the cabinet listing
options.c: Stored with up to 120 gallons of Class I liquids plus any additional quantity of Class II liquids
options.d: Shared with oxidizers if the oxidizers are kept on the bottom shelf

distractorExplanations.a: Open containers release vapor into the cabinet; containers must stay closed when not in use.
distractorExplanations.c: The 120-gallon cabinet limit covers Class I, II and IIIA liquids combined; Class II does not ride on top of it.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxidizers must be segregated from flammable liquids; shelf position within one cabinet is not separation.

options.a: A second listed cabinet placed beside the first, with no further room requirements
options.b: A sprinklered general warehouse area with 'No Smoking' signs posted at each entrance and exit door
options.c: An inside storage room with fire-resistive construction, ventilation, and spill containment
options.d: A room with natural ventilation through door louvers instead of mechanical exhaust

distractorExplanations.a: Multiple cabinets in one area are limited too; quantities above the limits require a code-compliant inside storage room.
distractorExplanations.b: General warehouse space with signage lacks the rated construction, ventilation and containment of an inside storage room.
distractorExplanations.d: Inside storage rooms for Class I liquids need designed ventilation, typically mechanical exhaust, not incidental door louvers.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: High-quantity storage needs rated construction, mechanical ventilation, containment, and electrical classification per NFPA 30. The room must be designed to code.

options.a: Pour rapidly so the transfer finishes before significant static charge builds up
options.b: Use a plastic funnel, since nonconductive materials cannot carry a static charge
options.c: Ground only the receiving container, then open the drum once flow is ready to start
options.d: Bond and ground containers before opening, maintaining contact throughout transfer

distractorExplanations.a: Faster flow generates more static charge; flow-rate control and bonding reduce the hazard, speed does not avoid it.
distractorExplanations.b: Nonconductive funnels accumulate charge and cannot be bonded; conductive, bonded equipment is required.
distractorExplanations.c: Both containers must be bonded and grounded before opening; grounding one side leaves a potential difference.

options.a: Understanding chemistry, operating limits, and independent protection layers
options.b: Operating close to alarm limits to maximize yield, relying on alarms to catch upsets
options.c: Bypassing interlocks during startup and night shifts when nuisance trips are frequent
options.d: Relying on experienced crews' verbal practices in place of written operating procedures

distractorExplanations.b: Running at alarm limits erodes safety margin; alarms are a protection layer, not a substitute for staying within limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Bypassed interlocks remove an independent protection layer; nuisance trips must be fixed, not bypassed.
distractorExplanations.d: Unwritten practices vary by crew; process safety requires written procedures with defined operating limits.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Process safety integrates design, procedures, training, and safeguards to prevent loss of containment and ignition of releases. Abnormal situation management is part of the same discipline.

options.a: A worn pump seal is replaced with an identical seal of the same specification
options.b: Process equipment, chemistry, utilities, or operating procedures change
options.c: Production runs at a higher rate that stays within established safe operating limits
options.d: An annual sprinkler inspection finds no deficiencies in the process building

distractorExplanations.a: That is replacement-in-kind, which is excluded from MOC because the design and specification do not change.
distractorExplanations.c: Operating within documented safe limits is not a change; MOC is triggered when limits, equipment or procedures change.
distractorExplanations.d: A routine inspection with no findings changes nothing in the process, so there is nothing for MOC to review.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: MOC evaluates unintended consequences of modifications to process technology, facilities, or organization affecting safety. The trigger is a change that could affect fire or explosion risk.

options.a: Replacement of a worn pump seal with an identical part of the same specification
options.b: Revision of the emergency contact list posted in the control room each year
options.c: Installation of a new solvent recovery unit with revised piping and interlocks
options.d: Routine filter replacement on unchanged equipment during a planned outage

distractorExplanations.a: Replacement-in-kind does not alter the process; PSSR is triggered by new facilities or modifications that change PSI.
distractorExplanations.b: Updating contact lists is administrative; it introduces no new equipment or hazards requiring pre-startup review.
distractorExplanations.d: Like-for-like filter changes are routine maintenance; PSSR applies to new or significantly modified process equipment.

options.a: High humidity from irrigation, which keeps plant material too wet to ignite
options.b: Carbon dioxide enrichment, which creates a flammable atmosphere in the room
options.c: Pesticide fogging residues, which form explosive dust clouds near light fixtures
options.d: High electrical load from lighting combined with combustible growing media

distractorExplanations.a: Moist plants still burn once dried by fire, and humidity does not prevent electrical ignition from overloaded circuits.
distractorExplanations.b: CO2 enrichment is an asphyxiation hazard, not a flammable atmosphere; the fire concern is electrical load and fuel.
distractorExplanations.c: Pesticide residues are a health concern; the leading grow-room fire cause is electrical overloading near combustible fuel.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Grow lighting, HVAC, extension wiring, and organic media create fuel and electrical ignition scenarios requiring engineered design and housekeeping. Limited egress in modified buildings compounds the risk.

options.a: Listed equipment, explosion-rated electrical in classified areas, ventilation, and gas detection
options.b: Open-loop extraction in a well-ventilated room, with a portable extinguisher at the booth
options.c: Spare butane cylinders stored inside the extraction room so they are close to the closed-loop unit
options.d: Standard general-purpose electrical, since the closed-loop system prevents vapor release

distractorExplanations.b: Open-loop hydrocarbon extraction is prohibited by NFPA 1 and the fire codes; listed closed-loop systems are required.
distractorExplanations.c: Solvent storage inside the extraction room adds fuel near ignition sources; storage quantities and locations are restricted.
distractorExplanations.d: Closed-loop systems can leak during changeovers; the extraction room needs classified electrical and gas detection.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Hydrocarbon extraction introduces flammable gas/vapor hazards requiring classified equipment, detection, and strict ignition controls. Hot work is prohibited in process spaces.

options.a: Clean agent total flooding as the sole protection, since it stops thermal runaway
options.b: Manufacturer emergency guidance, deflagration venting or spacing, and monitoring
options.c: Sealing enclosures airtight so flammable off-gas cannot reach the surrounding area
options.d: Treating batteries as an ordinary combustible commodity under NFPA 13 storage rules

distractorExplanations.a: Clean agents can knock down flame but do not stop cell-to-cell thermal runaway or remove off-gas hazards.
distractorExplanations.c: Sealed enclosures let off-gas accumulate to explosive concentrations; NFPA 855 requires explosion control or venting.
distractorExplanations.d: ESS installations are governed by NFPA 855 with specific spacing, size limits and explosion control, not commodity rules.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: ESS hazards include thermal runaway and off-gas; plans integrate detection, spacing, ventilation, and coordination with AHJ requirements. Combustible storage near the ESS should be restricted.

options.a: Sealing cabinet vents to keep the HVAC efficient and prevent dust from entering the battery modules
options.b: Silencing battery management alarms during charging cycles to reduce nuisance signals to the operators
options.c: Clearance maintenance, sprinkler or alternative suppression design per listing, and emergency response procedures
options.d: Clean agent suppression in every cabinet in place of written response procedures, since the agent stops thermal runaway

distractorExplanations.a: Blocking vents traps heat and flammable off-gas; listed ESS cabinets depend on designed ventilation or explosion control.
distractorExplanations.b: BMS alarms give early warning of cell abnormalities before thermal runaway; silencing them defeats detection.
distractorExplanations.d: Clean agent does not halt thermal runaway or off-gassing, and no suppression system replaces documented response plans.

options.a: Wetting the combustible floor once before welding begins
options.b: Covering the floor with cardboard as a disposable underlay
options.c: Lowering the welding current so slag cools before it reaches the floor
options.d: Fire-resistant blankets, shields, or noncombustible work surfaces

distractorExplanations.a: A single wetting dries quickly and wood still ignites; wetting is only a supplement to covers and a fire watch.
distractorExplanations.b: Cardboard is itself combustible; it adds fuel where slag lands instead of shielding the floor.
distractorExplanations.c: Current changes affect spatter but not slag temperature enough to protect combustible flooring; shielding is required.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Spark and slag travel farther than expected; shields and cleared areas are standard hot work controls. Combustibles should be relocated beyond spark travel distance.

options.a: Cleaning adjacent dust deposits, using dust-tight electrical equipment, and hot work permits
options.b: Wetting the dust deposits lightly and grinding at reduced speed to limit sparks
options.c: Directing sparks toward the floor, since settled dust cannot form an explosible cloud
options.d: Running local exhaust ventilation only, which captures the sparks before they can reach the dust

distractorExplanations.b: Light wetting dries out and lower speed still throws hot particles; deposits must be removed and permits used.
distractorExplanations.c: Sparks disturbing settled dust can raise a cloud and ignite it; layers also smolder and feed secondary explosions.
distractorExplanations.d: Exhaust pulls sparks into collectors where dust accumulates; it does not replace cleaning and hot work controls.

options.a: Recirculate filtered welding fumes back into the shop to conserve heated make-up air
options.b: Capture fumes at source without pulling sparks into combustible filters or ducts lacking spark traps
options.c: Use general dilution fans that blow the fumes and sparks away from the welder and toward the shop walls
options.d: Route exhaust ducts through concealed ceiling spaces to keep the shop floor clear

distractorExplanations.a: Recirculation is a health issue, and filters loaded with spark-laden fume are a fire risk; source capture with spark traps is preferred.
distractorExplanations.c: Fans can carry sparks toward combustibles; capture at source with spark arrest keeps sparks out of fuel areas.
distractorExplanations.d: Ducts in concealed combustible spaces can carry sparks into areas where fires go undetected.

options.a: Is performed by outside insurance surveyors in place of facility staff walkthroughs
options.b: Rotates randomly through areas without set frequencies so staff cannot prepare ahead
options.c: Uses standardized checklists, fixed frequencies, and documented corrective action tracking
options.d: Focuses on sprinkler and alarm equipment, leaving housekeeping and storage checks to the AHJ

distractorExplanations.a: Insurer surveys are periodic and external; self-inspection is an internal, frequent program owned by facility staff.
distractorExplanations.b: Unannounced checks have value, but self-inspection needs set frequencies so every area is covered consistently.
distractorExplanations.d: Self-inspection covers housekeeping, storage, ignition sources and egress, not just fire protection equipment.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Self-inspections detect housekeeping, storage, and procedural drift before incidents; documentation drives closure of deficiencies. Each item needs an accountable owner.

options.a: Clean floors with no ignition sources noted inside the mixing area
options.b: Closed, labeled solvent waste cans emptied at the end of shift
options.c: Functional eyewash station with clear access
options.d: Open solvent containers and blocked path to the fire extinguisher

distractorExplanations.a: A clean floor free of ignition sources is a satisfactory finding and requires no corrective action.
distractorExplanations.b: Closed, labeled waste cans emptied each shift reflect good practice, not a deficiency needing correction.
distractorExplanations.c: Closed labeled waste cans indicate good practice.

options.a: Identifying recurring deficiencies such as repeated hot work violations
options.b: Ranking each inspector's performance by the number of findings they record
options.c: Reducing inspection frequency in any area once one clean inspection is recorded
options.d: Supplying the data needed to set insurance premiums for the following year

distractorExplanations.b: Counting findings per inspector measures people, not hazards; trend analysis looks for repeating conditions.
distractorExplanations.c: A single clean result is not a trend; frequencies should change only on sustained data and hazard level.
distractorExplanations.d: Insurers may use loss data, but self-inspection trends exist to find systemic control failures to correct.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Recurring findings indicate systemic control failures needing engineering, procedure, or training intervention. Dust accumulating repeatedly in the same area is another example.

options.a: General-purpose outlets mounted at least 18 in. above the floor to stay above vapors
options.b: Electrical equipment rated for the classified area, plus prohibition of open flames
options.c: Sprinkler protection designed for Class I liquids, which removes ignition concerns
options.d: Plastic drum pumps that cannot spark, so bonding cables can be omitted during transfer

distractorExplanations.a: Mounting height does not make ordinary outlets safe; NFPA 70 requires equipment rated for the classified location.
distractorExplanations.c: Sprinklers control fire after ignition; they do not substitute for eliminating ignition sources in vapor areas.
distractorExplanations.d: Nonconductive pumps accumulate charge; bonding and grounding are still needed to prevent static discharge.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Classified electrical and ignition management prevent sparks in vapor-prone zones during normal and abnormal operations. Unapproved portable equipment is also prohibited.

options.a: Listed dust-ignition-proof vacuum with a conductive, grounded hose for Class II areas
options.b: Portable grounded dust collector listed for the Class II location
options.c: Unsealed conventional vacuum cleaner without dust-tight motor and grounding
options.d: Intrinsically safe portable lighting where required

distractorExplanations.a: A listed dust-ignition-proof vacuum with grounded hose is an acceptable control, so it is not the unacceptable device.
distractorExplanations.b: Equipment listed for the Class II location and grounded meets the requirement; it is an acceptable portable device.
distractorExplanations.d: Intrinsically safe lighting controls ignition in classified areas.

options.a: Lining metal chutes with plastic to insulate the flowing powder from the grounded conveying equipment
options.b: Increasing pneumatic conveying velocity so charged particles leave the system faster
options.c: Requiring operators to wear cotton clothing, with process equipment left ungrounded
options.d: Grounding and bonding of equipment, conductive flooring where needed, and humidity or ionization

distractorExplanations.a: Insulating liners let charge accumulate on the powder and isolated metal; grounding paths are needed to dissipate it.
distractorExplanations.b: Higher velocity increases triboelectric charging; velocity changes do not replace bonding and grounding.
distractorExplanations.c: Personnel controls help, but ungrounded equipment is the major static source in powder handling.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Static accumulates during flow and separation; grounding paths and facility design limit discharge energy in combustible atmospheres. Humidity or ionization controls are selected per assessment.

options.a: Placing them in listed self-closing metal containers emptied daily
options.b: Bagging them in sealed plastic bags inside a cardboard drum
options.c: Collecting them in an open steel drum emptied at the end of each week
options.d: Storing them in a covered bin beside the exit door for weekly pickup

distractorExplanations.b: Plastic bags and cardboard drums are combustible and trap oxidation heat; listed self-closing metal cans are required.
distractorExplanations.c: An open drum supplies oxygen and weekly emptying allows self-heating; containers must be self-closing and emptied daily.
distractorExplanations.d: Exit-side storage obstructs egress, and a weekly pickup lets heat build; daily removal in metal cans is expected.

options.a: Baled and kept beside electrical panels until the truck arrives
options.b: Removed on a scheduled basis to prevent ceiling-high piles
options.c: Stored in the stairwell if bins are labeled for recycling
options.d: Held until the annual deep clean when a contractor hauls it

distractorExplanations.a: Bales at electrical panels add fuel at an ignition source and block required working clearance.
distractorExplanations.c: Stairwells are egress paths; labeling does not permit combustible storage in exit enclosures.
distractorExplanations.d: Annual removal lets packaging waste build up for months, raising fire load and blocking sprinklers and aisles.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Excess combustible waste increases fire growth rate and can obstruct sprinklers and egress; frequent removal is basic prevention. Such piles exceed sprinkler design and block access.

options.a: Open belt conveyors routed through the spray finishing room to the outdoor bin
options.b: Floor piles along the exit route, swept up and carried to outdoor dumpsters at the end of each week
options.c: Covered ducts or direct chutes to metal collection drums located away from ignition sources
options.d: Plastic collection bags hung on each machine near the finish spray booth

distractorExplanations.a: Routing wood waste through the finishing room mixes fuel with flammable vapors and ignition sources.
distractorExplanations.b: Floor piles in egress paths block exits and build fuel load; enclosed transport to remote collection is required.
distractorExplanations.d: Plastic bags are combustible and accumulate static; placing them by the spray booth adds fuel near ignition.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Wood waste is fuel; enclosed transport and remote collection reduce dust and spark exposure near finishing ignition sources. Drums should be emptied regularly.

options.a: Visual confirmation that the tank is dry inside, followed by a standard hot work permit
options.b: Welding on the exterior only, since vapors inside cannot reach the weld zone
options.c: Filling the vessel with compressed air to purge vapors just before welding
options.d: Cleaning, gas testing, inerting or isolation as needed, and written authorization

distractorExplanations.a: Dry appearance does not prove absence of vapor; residues in seams and scale release flammable vapor when heated.
distractorExplanations.b: Heat conducts through the shell and can ignite interior vapor; exterior work still requires cleaning and testing.
distractorExplanations.c: Air purging can leave mixtures in the flammable range; inert gas or water filling is used, verified by gas testing.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Residual vapor in confined spaces creates explosion risk; cleaning, monitoring, and permits verify safe conditions. The authorization confirms safe entry and work conditions.

options.a: Preventing entrant exposure to welding fumes, toxic residues, and ignition of interior atmospheres
options.b: One combined permit for both crews, so that separate entry and hot work permits are no longer required
options.c: Ventilation fans running continuously, which make atmospheric monitoring optional
options.d: An attendant who also serves as the hot work fire watch to reduce crew size

distractorExplanations.b: Concurrent work needs both the entry permit and the hot work permit, coordinated, not merged into one.
distractorExplanations.c: Fans can fail or pull in contaminants; continuous or periodic gas monitoring is still required.
distractorExplanations.d: The attendant must focus on entrants; combining the role with fire watch compromises both duties.

options.a: Floor areas in walkways are swept, since dust above head height settles out
options.b: Horizontal and elevated surfaces are free of hazardous dust layers
options.c: Dust layers are acceptable where the dust matches the product color
options.d: Surfaces are cleaned with compressed air before corporate visits

distractorExplanations.a: Elevated beams and ducts hold the dust that fuels secondary explosions; audits must include them.
distractorExplanations.c: Color does not indicate depth or hazard; layers are judged against the measured accumulation threshold.
distractorExplanations.d: Compressed air raises dust clouds, and visit-driven cleaning lets layers build between audits.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Secondary deflagrations often involve dust on beams, ducts, and elevated surfaces; thresholds guide cleaning frequency. Layers are judged against the facility's established threshold.

options.a: Every year, with a complete DHA reanalysis after each internal compliance audit
options.b: Every three years, matching the OSHA PSM compliance audit cycle
options.c: Every five years, or when material, process, or building changes occur sooner
options.d: Every ten years, unless a dust fire or explosion occurs on site sooner

distractorExplanations.a: Annual reanalysis is not the NFPA 652 interval; the DHA must be reviewed at least every five years.
distractorExplanations.b: Three years is the PSM compliance audit interval; NFPA 652 sets five years for DHA review.
distractorExplanations.d: Ten years is too long, and waiting for an incident ignores process changes that require revalidation.

options.a: Into an adjacent unoccupied room through a vent duct longer than 20 ft to absorb pressure
options.b: Toward the employee parking lot, since the vehicles there are unoccupied for most of the work shift
options.c: At a neighboring dust collector so the pressure wave is shared and reduced between units
options.d: To a safe exterior area away from occupied paths, vehicles, and additional fuel concentrations

distractorExplanations.a: Long vent ducts raise reduced pressure in the vessel and discharge flame indoors; ducts are kept short and outdoors.
distractorExplanations.b: Vented fireballs can reach people and vehicles; the discharge zone must be kept clear of occupied areas.
distractorExplanations.c: Venting onto another collector can damage it and ignite its dust, spreading the event.

options.a: Approved pumps or self-closing faucets, drip containment, and quantities limited to daily use
options.b: Open dip tanks left uncovered during the shift so parts can be cleaned quickly between production batches
options.c: A week's supply in open trays at each bench to reduce trips to the storage room
options.d: Gravity pouring from 55-gallon drums on the bench, with bonding used for Class II only

distractorExplanations.b: Uncovered dip tanks release vapor continuously; dip tanks need covers, and NFPA 34 controls apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Bench quantities are limited to daily use in closed containers; open trays release vapor.
distractorExplanations.d: Class I liquids need bonding most; drum dispensing at benches without bonding risks static ignition.

options.a: Water-wash booths alone, which make ventilation interlocks and filter changes unnecessary
options.b: Ventilation, elimination of ignition sources, and maintenance of spray booths and filters
options.c: Portable heaters inside the booth to keep coatings warm and lower solvent viscosity
options.d: Spraying with the exhaust fan off to reduce overspray loss to the filters

distractorExplanations.a: Water-wash booths capture overspray but still need ventilation, interlocks and residue cleaning under NFPA 33.
distractorExplanations.c: Unlisted heaters inside booths are ignition sources in a Class I Division 1 area.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 33 interlocks spraying to exhaust airflow; without it, vapors exceed safe concentrations.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Overspray creates flammable atmospheres; ventilation and ignition control maintain concentrations below dangerous levels. Proper solvent storage is also part of the program.

options.a: Sealing return air paths to contain odor, with excess heat managed by propping doors open
options.b: Extension cords to power portable dehumidifiers as rooms are added
options.c: Filter maintenance, duct cleanliness, and electrical loading of dehumidification units
options.d: Placing condensate drains beside electrical panels for easy inspection

distractorExplanations.a: Blocked returns overheat equipment; odor control uses filtration, not sealing airflow paths.
distractorExplanations.b: Extension cords used as permanent wiring overload and overheat; dehumidifiers need properly sized circuits.
distractorExplanations.d: Water near panels causes faults and arcing; condensate should be routed away from electrical equipment.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: HVAC in grow environments handles dust, moisture, and high load; poor maintenance creates fuel and electrical ignition potential. Clearance to combustible finishes also matters.

options.a: Ornamental landscaping planted against the cabinets to screen them from view
options.b: Placement inside a fenced yard with locked gates and no fire department access
options.c: Siting directly against the building wall to shorten cable runs to the main electrical switchgear
options.d: Exposure separation from buildings, vegetation management, and access for emergency cooling

distractorExplanations.a: Vegetation against ESS cabinets is fuel for exposure fires; NFPA 855 requires a cleared zone.
distractorExplanations.b: Security fencing must still allow responder access for monitoring, cooling and isolation.
distractorExplanations.c: NFPA 855 requires separation from buildings and openings to limit exposure fire spread.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Separation and clear access support exposure control and emergency response; vegetation and vehicles can introduce external fire exposure. Access for isolation per the AHJ is also needed.

options.a: Guards are in place and sparks are directed away from combustibles
options.b: Guards are removed so the operator can see the cutting edge
options.c: The wheel diameter fits the arbor, with speed rating checked yearly
options.d: Sparks are directed toward the floor drain, where oil collects

distractorExplanations.b: Removing guards exposes the operator to wheel burst and lets sparks spray in any direction.
distractorExplanations.c: Fit is not enough; each wheel's rated speed must meet or exceed the machine speed before mounting.
distractorExplanations.d: Directing sparks toward oil residues invites ignition; sparks must go away from fuels and oils.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Wheel burst and spark ejection hazards require proper guards, speed rating, and spark direction away from fuels. The wheel must also be compatible with machine speed.

options.a: Secondary containment is omitted where floors are sealed concrete
options.b: Containers are closed, labeled, and within quantity limits for the space
options.c: Minor leaks under one gallon per day are logged for the next audit
options.d: Oxidizers share shelving with flammable liquids if each container is labeled clearly

distractorExplanations.a: Sealed floors do not contain spills; containment or drainage is required where codes apply.
distractorExplanations.c: Any leak must be corrected promptly; tolerating daily leaks sustains flammable vapors.
distractorExplanations.d: Labels do not separate incompatibles; oxidizers need segregation from flammable liquids.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Inspections confirm NFPA 30 fundamentals: containment, segregation, labeling, and quantity control. Containers must also be segregated from incompatible materials.

options.a: Removing flame arrestors temporarily to increase vent flow during nitrogen line purging
options.b: Hot work on lines once they are drained, with isolation verified at restart
options.c: Lockout/tagout of energy sources, hot work permits, and flammable atmosphere testing
options.d: Restarting before leak checks, then completing them during normal operation

distractorExplanations.a: Removing arrestors lets flame propagate into vent piping exactly when flammable mixtures are present.
distractorExplanations.b: Isolation and gas testing must be verified before hot work, not deferred until restart.
distractorExplanations.d: Leak checks must precede startup so flammable releases are found before process fluids are introduced.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Outages introduce simultaneous mechanical and hot work; energy isolation and gas testing prevent ignition during recommissioning. Atmosphere testing is done before startup.

options.a: Accepting spent lithium batteries in the charge chamber to lower separate disposal costs for the site
options.b: Bypassing the chamber heat sensor when it trips during high-volume shifts
options.c: Storing open hydraulic fluid containers on the compactor for top-ups
options.d: Routine cleaning of buildup, sprinkler protection per design, and prohibiting hot or reactive wastes

distractorExplanations.a: Crushing lithium batteries causes internal shorts and thermal runaway inside the compactor.
distractorExplanations.b: Bypassing heat sensors removes early warning of smoldering waste in the charge chamber.
distractorExplanations.c: Open hydraulic oil on the unit adds a flammable fuel source next to compaction equipment.

options.a: Coordinate hot work, housekeeping, dust management, and training under accountable management review
options.b: Assign each hazard program to a separate department, each with its own independent audit schedule and budget
options.c: Rely on annual insurance carrier surveys to set priorities in place of internal inspections
options.d: Concentrate resources on post-incident investigation to identify which controls to add next

distractorExplanations.b: Siloed programs miss interactions such as hot work near dust; integration requires coordinated oversight.
distractorExplanations.c: Insurer surveys supplement but cannot replace internal ownership, self-inspection and management review.
distractorExplanations.d: Investigation is reactive; prevention programs must act before losses through proactive controls.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Effective programs link controls across fuels, ignition sources, and processes with leadership oversight and continuous improvement. Flammable liquids and self-inspection are coordinated the same way.

options.a: Items with the lowest correction cost, so the most deficiencies close quickly
options.b: Conditions that combine immediate ignition likelihood with life safety impact
options.c: Deficiencies cited most often in past insurance surveys, in date order
options.d: Administrative gaps such as overdue training records and expired permits on file

distractorExplanations.a: Cost-based ordering ignores risk; imminent ignition with egress impact is corrected first.
distractorExplanations.c: Historical citation frequency does not equal current risk; prioritization is by likelihood and consequence.
distractorExplanations.d: Records gaps matter but carry less immediate consequence than active ignition sources near blocked exits.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-prevention-pro.explanation: Risk-based prioritization addresses imminent ignition-egress scenarios before lower-consequence aesthetic or administrative items. Example: blocked exits with active hot work nearby.

options.a: Moderate quantities of combustibles with low heat release
options.b: Low quantities of combustibles with low heat release, such as offices and churches
options.c: High quantities of combustibles with stockpiles over 12 ft, such as paper mills
options.d: Flammable liquids in significant amounts, such as solvent cleaning and dip tanks

distractorExplanations.b: That describes light hazard occupancies such as offices, churches and schools, not Ordinary Hazard Group 1.
distractorExplanations.c: Stockpiles above 12 ft and high fuel loads point to extra hazard or storage criteria, not Ordinary Hazard Group 1.
distractorExplanations.d: Significant flammable liquid use describes Extra Hazard Group 2 occupancies, not Ordinary Hazard Group 1.

cfps-readiness-check-fire-suppression-00.explanation: OH1 includes spaces with moderate fuel loads and low heat release rates; hazard classification drives sprinkler design density and area. Examples include light manufacturing and mechanical rooms.

options.a: 0.05 gpm/ft² over the hydraulically most remote 1,500 ft² design area
options.b: 0.10 gpm/ft² over the hydraulically most remote 1,500 ft² design area
options.c: 0.15 gpm/ft² over the hydraulically most remote 1,500 ft² design area
options.d: 0.20 gpm/ft² over the hydraulically most remote 1,500 ft² design area

distractorExplanations.a: 0.05 gpm/ft² is below any NFPA 13 density curve; the light hazard design point starts at 0.10 gpm/ft².
distractorExplanations.c: 0.15 gpm/ft² over 1,500 ft² is the Ordinary Hazard Group 1 design point, not light hazard.
distractorExplanations.d: 0.20 gpm/ft² over 1,500 ft² is the Ordinary Hazard Group 2 design point, above light hazard density.

options.a: Provide control-mode density/area protection for ordinary hazard offices using standard-response heads
options.b: Protect high-piled storage under ceilings of any height, since ESFR has no maximum ceiling height limit
options.c: Control or suppress high-challenge storage fires without in-rack sprinklers in many rack configurations
options.d: Protect open-top container and solid-shelf rack storage where ceiling sprinklers cannot reach the fire

distractorExplanations.a: ESFR heads are fast-response suppression-mode sprinklers for storage; density/area control with standard-response heads describes CMDA protection.
distractorExplanations.b: ESFR listings and NFPA 13 tables cap ceiling and storage heights (e.g., 45 ft ceilings); above those limits ESFR is not permitted.
distractorExplanations.d: Open-top containers and solid shelving block ESFR penetration; NFPA 13 generally prohibits ESFR for these unless in-rack protection is added.

options.a: Piping filled with pressurized air or nitrogen, with water entering only after a sprinkler opens
options.b: Piping kept empty of water, with water admitted when a separate detection system opens the control valve
options.c: Open sprinklers on dry piping, with water released to every head when a deluge valve trips
options.d: Piping filled with water under pressure, with water discharged immediately when a sprinkler operates

distractorExplanations.a: Pressurized air or nitrogen that holds water back until a sprinkler opens defines a dry pipe system, not a wet pipe system.
distractorExplanations.b: Empty piping filled on detector operation describes a preaction system; a wet system has water at the sprinklers at all times.
distractorExplanations.c: Open heads discharging together when a valve trips is a deluge system; wet systems use closed heads that operate individually.

options.a: Hold the dry pipe valve closed and monitor for leaks while keeping piping free of water until activation
options.b: Pressurize the piping so that water reaches the most remote sprinkler faster after a sprinkler head opens
options.c: Provide the motive force that pushes water through the system once the dry pipe valve trips
