distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 1710 sets 480 seconds (8 minutes), not 10, as the travel time for the initial full alarm assignment.

options.a: Counting mutual aid personnel only when they arrive within NFPA 1710 times
options.b: Reducing interior crews to two members when callback staffing is slow
options.c: An effective response force assembled from on-duty, on-call, or callback personnel
options.d: Exempting departments in rural demand zones from any staffing or response time objectives

distractorExplanations.a: NFPA 1720 uses its own demand-zone assembly times, not the NFPA 1710 career travel-time objectives.
distractorExplanations.b: Two-member interior crews violate two-in/two-out; NFPA 1720 does not relax minimum interior team safety.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 1720 still sets rural demand-zone objectives (6 staff within 14 minutes, 80% of the time), not exemptions.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: NFPA 1720 accommodates volunteer models using assembly of available personnel while still setting deployment benchmarks. The force is assembled within defined time frames.

options.a: Document code violations for citation during the next fire inspection
options.b: Set the fire insurance rating for the property under ISO grading
options.c: Predetermine the IC's strategy so on-scene size-up can be shortened
options.d: Identify building hazards, access points, and tactical considerations

distractorExplanations.a: Citing violations is a code enforcement function; pre-plans gather tactical intelligence for operations.
distractorExplanations.b: ISO's Public Protection Classification rates community fire protection; it is not the purpose of a pre-incident plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Pre-plans inform but do not replace on-scene size-up, because actual conditions differ from planned assumptions.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Pre-plans provide critical intelligence on construction, occupancy, hydrants, and FDC locations to support faster, safer operations. This intelligence is gathered before an emergency occurs.

options.a: Standpipe and FDC locations, elevator recall features, and stairwell configuration
options.b: Annual inspection violation history, permit dates, and the owner's insurance policy
options.c: Ground-floor contents inventory, salvage cover needs, and overhaul staging areas
options.d: Sprinkler head counts per floor, ceiling tile type, and lobby furniture layout

distractorExplanations.b: Inspection and insurance records are administrative files; high-rise pre-plans focus on systems and vertical access.
distractorExplanations.c: Salvage and overhaul details are secondary; a high-rise plan prioritizes standpipes, FDCs, elevators and stairs.
distractorExplanations.d: Head counts and finishes are design minutiae; the plan needs standpipe/FDC locations, elevator recall and stair layout.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: High-rise pre-plans focus on fire protection systems, egress, vertical access, and ventilation considerations critical to strategy. Occupant notification systems belong in the plan as well.

options.a: Every five years on a fixed cycle tied to the community's ISO grading schedule
options.b: When significant changes occur to construction, occupancy, or protection systems
options.c: When the property changes ownership, management company, or insurance carrier
options.d: After each fire department response to an alarm at the property

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed multi-year cycle can miss renovations or occupancy changes in between; updates follow significant change.
distractorExplanations.c: Ownership or insurer changes do not alter fire conditions; physical, occupancy or system changes drive updates.
distractorExplanations.d: Response frequency is not the trigger; a plan can be stale without any alarms if the building was modified.

options.a: Rely mainly on fear-based images of fire deaths to motivate change
options.b: Deliver one general fire safety message to every audience in the same way each year
options.c: Target specific behaviors such as smoke alarm maintenance and escape planning
options.d: Focus on station open houses and apparatus displays to build goodwill

distractorExplanations.a: Fear appeals without specific actions rarely change behavior; effective programs teach concrete safe behaviors.
distractorExplanations.b: Uniform messaging ignores audience risk; effective programs tailor content to high-risk groups and behaviors.
distractorExplanations.d: Open houses build relations but measure no behavior change; education should target specific risk behaviors.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Evidence-based public education addresses identifiable fire causes and behaviors, reaching audiences at highest risk. Cooking fire prevention is another typical target behavior.

options.a: National fire statistics and the NFPA annual calendar of campaign themes
options.b: Requests from community groups and schools for station tours and talks
options.c: The insurance industry's property loss rankings for commercial occupancies
options.d: Local fire loss data, demographic profiles, and identified community hazards

distractorExplanations.a: National themes are useful supplements, but priorities should come from local loss data and community risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Demand-driven scheduling reaches whoever asks, not the highest-risk populations identified by data.
distractorExplanations.c: Commercial property loss rankings miss the residential life-safety risk behind most civilian fire deaths.

options.a: Enforcement, engineering, economic incentives, and emergency response
options.b: Evacuation drills, equipment testing, and emergency medical training
options.c: Inspection, investigation, and insurance rating improvement programs
options.d: Emergency management, evacuation planning, and environmental review

distractorExplanations.b: Drills and testing are activities, not CRR elements; CRR pairs education with enforcement, engineering, incentives and response.
distractorExplanations.c: Inspection and investigation are inputs; the CRR model is the five E's: education, enforcement, engineering, economic incentives, emergency response.
distractorExplanations.d: Those are emergency-management functions; the CRR E's are education, enforcement, engineering, economic incentives and emergency response.

options.a: The officer who commands every incident personally from first alarm on
options.b: The executive head responsible for department administration and policy
options.c: An official elected by voters and independent of municipal management
options.d: The head of the fire prevention bureau and chief fire investigator

distractorExplanations.a: Chiefs may assume command at major incidents, but initial command is held by first-arriving officers.
distractorExplanations.c: Most municipal chiefs are appointed and report to a city manager or mayor; elected independence is uncommon.
distractorExplanations.d: Fire prevention and investigation are led by a fire marshal or division chief, not the Fire Chief's core role.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: The Fire Chief leads the department, reports to a city manager or mayor, and sets policy, budgets, and strategic priorities. The chief also sets strategic direction.

options.a: Supervises the companies on one shift within an assigned geographic battalion
options.b: Leads a single company and its crew at the station level
options.c: Manages a major functional area such as operations, prevention, or training
options.d: Serves as the department's designated Incident Safety Officer on every working alarm

distractorExplanations.a: Shift supervision of companies in a battalion is the battalion chief's role, not the division chief's.
distractorExplanations.b: Leading a single company is the company officer's (captain or lieutenant) role, two levels below.
distractorExplanations.d: The ISO is an assigned incident role; division chiefs manage functional program areas of the department.

options.a: Managing a department-wide program such as training or prevention
options.b: Leading one company's crew and apparatus during daily operations
options.c: Setting department policy and budget as the executive head
options.d: Supervising multiple companies and managing shift operations

distractorExplanations.a: Department-wide programs are run by division or deputy chiefs; battalion chiefs supervise companies on shift.
distractorExplanations.b: Running one company is the company officer's job; a battalion chief supervises several companies.
distractorExplanations.c: Department policy and budget belong to the Fire Chief as the executive head of the department.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Battalion chiefs bridge line operations and administration, directing companies and assuming command at escalating incidents. They also serve as an initial Incident Commander at major alarms.

options.a: Direct supervision of personnel, apparatus, and operations at the company level
options.b: Supervision of several companies and shift operations across an assigned battalion
options.c: Management of a functional division such as training or fire prevention
options.d: Department budget preparation and adoption of the local fire code

distractorExplanations.b: Multi-company shift supervision describes a battalion chief, not a captain or lieutenant.
distractorExplanations.c: Functional divisions are led by division chiefs, a level above company officers.
distractorExplanations.d: Budgets are prepared by the chief's office and codes are adopted by the governing body, not company officers.

options.a: Minimum staffing and response-time objectives for career companies
options.b: A comprehensive occupational safety and health program
options.c: A community risk reduction plan based on local fire loss data
options.d: Professional qualification levels for fire officers I through IV

distractorExplanations.a: Staffing and response time objectives come from NFPA 1710, not from NFPA 1500.
distractorExplanations.c: CRR planning is addressed in NFPA 1300, not in the occupational safety standard NFPA 1500.
distractorExplanations.d: Fire Officer I through IV qualifications are in NFPA 1021 (now NFPA 1020), not NFPA 1500.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: NFPA 1500 mandates formal safety programs including hazard identification, PPE, medical surveillance, and incident safety roles. The program includes written policies, training, and enforcement.

options.a: Training only, since PPE is issued solely by the EMS agency
options.b: Annual training, with medical follow-up after a confirmed infection
options.c: Appropriate training, PPE, medical evaluation, and follow-up
options.d: PPE and vaccination, with training covered by EMT certification

distractorExplanations.a: PPE is a department obligation under NFPA 1500 and OSHA bloodborne pathogen rules, not left to an EMS agency.
distractorExplanations.b: Post-exposure evaluation must follow the exposure incident itself, not wait for a confirmed infection.
distractorExplanations.d: EMT certification does not replace the department's infection control training under NFPA 1500 and OSHA 1910.1030.

options.a: The Operations Section Chief, who already oversees crews
options.b: The Incident Commander, who retains overall safety responsibility
options.c: The RIC team leader, who is staged near the entry point
options.d: A qualified individual dedicated to safety monitoring

distractorExplanations.a: Combining ISO with Operations removes the independent safety oversight NFPA 1521 intends.
distractorExplanations.b: The IC keeps overall safety responsibility but should delegate the ISO role once the incident expands.
distractorExplanations.c: The RIC leader must stay ready for firefighter rescue; diverting them to ISO duties weakens both functions.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: NFPA 1521 requires a qualified ISO; combining ISO with Operations creates conflicts and exceeds span of control. The ISO should not simultaneously serve as Operations Section Chief.

options.a: Conduct risk assessment and apply risk management principles
options.b: Assign all safety decisions to the Incident Safety Officer
options.c: Complete a written incident action plan before the first alarm clears
options.d: Remain inside the structure to supervise interior crews directly

distractorExplanations.b: The ISO advises and can stop unsafe acts, but NFPA 1561 keeps risk management responsibility with the IC.
distractorExplanations.c: Written IAPs are needed for extended or complex incidents, not every first alarm; the core duty is risk management.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 1561 favors a fixed, stationary command post outside the hazard area, not interior positioning.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: NFPA 1561 integrates risk management into command decisions, balancing operational needs with firefighter safety. Risk management continues throughout the incident.

options.a: Continued offensive attack with an additional RIC team assigned
options.b: Transition to defensive operations and withdrawal of personnel
options.c: Interior crews held in place while the ISO reassesses conditions
options.d: Rotation of fresh crews into the same interior positions

distractorExplanations.a: Adding a RIC does not make unacceptable risk acceptable; the IC must change strategy and withdraw crews.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding crews in an untenable position delays withdrawal; risk management requires removing them.
distractorExplanations.d: Fresh crews face the same unacceptable risk; crew rotation addresses fatigue, not the hazard level.

options.a: An annual refresher covering hazmat awareness and bloodborne pathogens
options.b: Initial academy training, with refreshers left to individual members
options.c: Job performance requirements for assigned duties and safety procedures
options.d: Live-fire evolutions as the primary method of continuing training

distractorExplanations.a: Those are just two annual topics; NFPA 1500 requires training tied to every assigned duty plus proficiency upkeep.
distractorExplanations.b: Continuing training is a department obligation under NFPA 1500, not optional self-study.
distractorExplanations.d: Live fire is one method under NFPA 1403 controls; training must cover all job performance requirements.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: NFPA 1500 requires comprehensive initial and continuing training tied to job performance requirements and safety. Regular proficiency maintenance is also required.

options.a: Fire officer supervision, incident command, and crew evaluations
options.b: Hazmat technician-level product control and decontamination
options.c: Interior fire attack, search, and ventilation as Firefighter II
options.d: Apparatus operation, pumping, and safe positioning on the fireground

distractorExplanations.a: Supervision and command are NFPA 1021 fire officer competencies, not driver/operator job performance requirements.
distractorExplanations.b: Hazmat technician skills are NFPA 1072 competencies, not part of driver/operator qualification.
distractorExplanations.c: Search and interior attack are NFPA 1001 firefighter JPRs; NFPA 1002 focuses on driving and operating apparatus.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Driver/operators must demonstrate mechanical operation, hydraulics, and scene positioning relevant to their assigned apparatus. Aerial device operation is included where the apparatus is so equipped.

options.a: Fire Officer I through IV competencies covering supervision and management
options.b: Firefighter I and II competencies followed by Driver/Operator certification
options.c: Incident Safety Officer and Health and Safety Officer qualification levels
options.d: Fire Inspector I through III competencies and Plans Examiner qualifications

distractorExplanations.b: Firefighter I/II and driver/operator are NFPA 1001/1002 levels, not the fire officer progression.
distractorExplanations.c: ISO and HSO qualifications are in NFPA 1521, separate from the NFPA 1021 Fire Officer levels.
distractorExplanations.d: Inspector and plans examiner levels are NFPA 1031 qualifications, not NFPA 1021 fire officer levels.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: NFPA 1021 defines progressive officer competencies from company-level supervision to executive administration. Fire Officer IV covers executive leadership.

options.a: Two firefighters enter while one remains outside at the entry point
options.b: At least two firefighters enter together while two remain outside
options.c: Two companies of two firefighters each enter for interior attack
options.d: Two firefighters enter after two more complete a 360° size-up

distractorExplanations.a: A single outside member does not meet OSHA 1910.134; at least two must stand by outside.
distractorExplanations.c: Sending all four inside leaves no outside standby team, defeating the two-out requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: A 360° size-up is good practice, but the rule requires two members outside standing by for rescue during entry.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: OSHA 1910.134 and fire service practice require a standby team equal to interior team size for immediate rescue capability. The two outside remain available for rescue.

options.a: Once a second alarm is struck at the incident
options.b: When the IC declares the incident a defensive operation
options.c: Before interior firefighting operations begin
options.d: Immediately after a mayday is transmitted by interior crews

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for a second alarm leaves first-alarm interior crews without dedicated rescue capability.
distractorExplanations.b: In defensive operations nobody is in the IDLH atmosphere; RIC is needed before interior entry begins.
distractorExplanations.d: Forming a team after a mayday wastes critical minutes; the RIC must be staged before entry.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: RIC/FAST teams must be staged and ready prior to interior entry to provide immediate rescue if a firefighter emergency occurs. This applies at structural incidents where members enter the IDLH environment.

options.a: By radio to dispatch, with the new IC briefed after the fire is controlled
options.b: Upon arrival of the highest-ranking officer, without a formal briefing
options.c: In writing on the ICS 201 form before any verbal briefing
options.d: Face-to-face with a briefing when possible, documenting the time

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying the briefing until control leaves the new IC directing operations without situation status.
distractorExplanations.b: Rank alone does not transfer command; the arriving officer must be briefed and the transfer announced.
distractorExplanations.c: The ICS 201 supports the briefing, but transfer happens by face-to-face or radio briefing, not paperwork first.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Effective transfer includes direct communication of situation status, current actions, resource assignments, and safety concerns. Conditions at the time of transfer are documented too.

options.a: Coordinating with cooperating and assisting agency representatives
options.b: Releasing incident information to the media and the public
options.c: Monitoring hazards and stopping unsafe acts on the fireground
options.d: Tracking resource check-in, status, and incident documentation

distractorExplanations.b: Media and public information is the Public Information Officer's role, not the Liaison Officer's.
distractorExplanations.c: Hazard monitoring and stopping unsafe acts is the Safety Officer's command staff role.
distractorExplanations.d: Check-in and status tracking belong to the Planning Section's Resources Unit, not command staff.

options.a: Release casualty details as soon as crews report them to command
options.b: Provide accurate, timely information to the public and media
options.c: Coordinate with representatives from assisting and cooperating agencies
options.d: Approve all press releases issued by assisting agencies independently

distractorExplanations.a: Casualty information must be verified, next of kin notified, and release approved by the IC first.
distractorExplanations.c: Coordinating agency representatives is the Liaison Officer's function, not the PIO's.
distractorExplanations.d: The PIO coordinates messages with the IC and partner PIOs in a Joint Information Center but does not approve them alone.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: The PIO manages external communications, ensuring consistency with command objectives and verified facts. Messages are coordinated with command.

options.a: Station design standards, apparatus specifications, and replacement cycles
options.b: Annual training calendars, certification renewals, and promotional exams
options.c: Apparatus staging, callback procedures, and coverage of vacated stations
options.d: Hydrant inspection routes, flow testing, and water main maintenance

distractorExplanations.a: Facility and fleet standards are capital planning, not the deployment plan for escalating incidents.
distractorExplanations.b: Training and promotion schedules are administrative; deployment plans address coverage and resource movement.
distractorExplanations.d: Hydrant maintenance is a water supply program, not resource deployment during major incidents.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Deployment plans ensure adequate coverage, resource accountability, and strategic placement during escalated incidents. Resource typing also belongs in the plan for major incidents.

options.a: Upgrade the incident to unified command with neighboring jurisdictions
options.b: Notify the state fire marshal that a cause investigation is needed
options.c: Signal the transition from offensive to defensive operations
options.d: Request additional resources to match escalating incident demands

distractorExplanations.a: Additional alarms add resources; unified command depends on multiple jurisdictions with authority.
distractorExplanations.b: Investigation notification is separate from alarm levels, which dispatch preassigned resources.
distractorExplanations.c: Strategy changes are announced by the IC; striking alarms requests more resources in either mode.

options.a: Responding units meet defined capability and equipment standards
options.b: Each department's apparatus are billed at a uniform reimbursement rate
options.c: Units arrive in the order they are listed on the run card
options.d: Resources are assigned to the closest jurisdiction's command

distractorExplanations.b: Reimbursement is set by agreements and cost rules; typing defines capability, not billing rates.
distractorExplanations.c: Run card order is dispatch sequencing; typing defines the minimum capabilities of each resource category.
distractorExplanations.d: Command assignment is an ICS decision; typing standardizes what a requested resource can do.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Typing (e.g., Type 1 engine) standardizes expectations so requesting agencies receive appropriate capabilities. The standards apply to the requested resource category.

options.a: Require written approval from the chief before any deviation occurs
options.b: Provide consistent operational procedures while allowing deviation
options.c: Prescribe a fixed tactic for each occupancy type so judgment is not needed
options.d: Serve as training references only, with no effect on operations

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-approval is impractical on the fireground; SOGs let the IC deviate and document the reason.
distractorExplanations.c: SOGs standardize common actions but rely on trained officer judgment for conditions they cannot anticipate.
distractorExplanations.d: SOGs are operational directives, not just training references; they guide actual incident procedures.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: SOGs/SOPs standardize common operations; the IC may deviate with documented justification when conditions warrant. Deviation is allowed when conditions require IC judgment.

options.a: Assigning units in fixed station-number order for every call type
options.b: Routing every call to the IC for approval before units are dispatched
options.c: Coordinating call taking, automatic aid dispatch, and unit recommendation
options.d: Separating fire and EMS call taking into independent answering points

distractorExplanations.a: Fixed order ignores location; integrated CAD recommends the closest appropriate unit using AVL and GIS.
distractorExplanations.b: IC approval before dispatch adds delay; CAD dispatches per pre-programmed run cards.
distractorExplanations.d: Separate answering points add transfer delays; integration consolidates call taking across agencies.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: CAD and integrated dispatch reduce dispatch times and assign appropriate resources using pre-programmed run cards and GIS. Recommendations are based on location and call type.

options.a: Maximum consecutive duty hours to cut overtime and staffing costs
options.b: Seniority bidding as the main factor in assigning crews
options.c: Rotating overnight shifts weekly so every member shares night work
options.d: Adequate rest, fatigue management, and coverage requirements

distractorExplanations.a: Extended duty without rest raises fatigue-related error and injury; cost cannot override fatigue management.
distractorExplanations.b: Seniority bidding is a labor practice; schedules must first ensure adequate rest and station coverage.
distractorExplanations.c: Frequent rotation disrupts circadian rhythm and increases fatigue; it is not a fatigue control.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Fatigue management under NFPA 1500 and labor practices affects response readiness and firefighter safety. Labor agreements and safety standards also apply.

options.a: Completion of required initial and continuing training for each member
options.b: Attendance hours logged for each member, without any skills verification
options.c: Training records for officers and specialty team members
options.d: Course completions for state certification, kept only by the state agency

distractorExplanations.b: Hours alone do not show competency; records must show completed training and skills for assigned duties.
distractorExplanations.c: Every member needs documented training for assigned duties, not just officers or specialty teams.
distractorExplanations.d: State certification files do not replace the department's own records of initial and continuing training.

cfps-readiness-check-organizing-fire-res.explanation: Training documentation supports ISO audits, certification maintenance, and legal defensibility of department preparedness. Records should match each member's assigned duties.

options.a: Adopting the career department's SOGs for every responding unit on arrival
options.b: Clear command structure, interoperable communications, and joint training
options.c: Assigning the career department command because of its staffing
options.d: Separate operating areas so each department can use its own familiar tactics

distractorExplanations.a: Imposing one department's SOGs without joint training ignores differences; coordination comes from ICS and drills.
distractorExplanations.c: Command is based on jurisdiction and qualifications, not on whether a department is career or volunteer.
distractorExplanations.d: Separating departments without unified objectives creates freelancing; a common command structure is needed.

options.a: Exit access, exit, and exit discharge
options.b: Exit access, exit enclosure, and refuge area
options.c: Corridor, protected stair, and public way
options.d: Common path, travel distance, and exit width

distractorExplanations.b: Exit enclosures and refuge areas are features; the three-part NFPA 101 model ends with exit discharge.
distractorExplanations.c: The public way is the destination, not a component; the three parts are exit access, exit and exit discharge.
distractorExplanations.d: Those are egress measurements and limits, not the three components of a means of egress.

options.a: Counting the employees and visitors present at the busiest hour
options.b: Dividing the floor area by the occupant load factor for the use
options.c: Multiplying the number of exits by their combined clear width
options.d: Dividing the floor area by the plumbing fixture ratio for the use

distractorExplanations.a: Actual counts matter only if they exceed the calculated load; the baseline is area divided by the factor.
distractorExplanations.c: Exit width determines egress capacity, which must accommodate occupant load; it does not calculate it.
distractorExplanations.d: Plumbing fixture ratios come from plumbing codes; NFPA 101 uses occupant load factors by use.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: NFPA 101 assigns occupant load factors by use/occupancy; area divided by factor yields required design occupant load. Code rounding rules are then applied.

options.a: Seats sold for the event plus the staff working in the seating area
options.b: The seating area divided by 7 net square feet per person, ignoring the actual seat count
options.c: All fixed seats plus any standing-room areas calculated separately by area factor
options.d: Fixed seats only, with standing room excluded from the occupant load

distractorExplanations.a: Ticket sales reflect one event; design occupant load uses the number of installed fixed seats.
distractorExplanations.b: 7 net sq ft applies to concentrated use without fixed seats; fixed seating uses the actual seat count.
distractorExplanations.d: Standing-room areas add to occupant load and must be calculated by the applicable area factor.

options.a: In a straight line from the most remote point to the nearest exit
options.b: Along the egress path from the most remote point all the way to the public way
options.c: Along the egress path from the most remote point to the farthest available exit
options.d: Along the natural egress path from the most remote point to the nearest exit

distractorExplanations.a: Straight-line measurement through walls is not permitted; travel distance follows the actual walking path.
distractorExplanations.b: Travel distance ends at an exit (such as a stair door), not at the public way after exit discharge.
distractorExplanations.c: Travel distance is measured to the nearest exit, not to the farthest one.

options.a: The portion of exit access before two separate egress paths become available
options.b: The corridor length beyond an exit or corridor intersection with no outlet
options.c: The total distance from the most remote point to the nearest exit
options.d: The distance between two exits measured along the diagonal of the space

distractorExplanations.b: A corridor portion with no exit beyond it describes a dead end, not common path of travel.
distractorExplanations.c: That is travel distance; common path is only the initial portion before the paths split.
distractorExplanations.d: Exit separation along the diagonal is the remoteness rule (one-half or one-third diagonal), not common path.

options.a: 0.2 inches of clear width per occupant
options.b: 0.3 inches of clear width per occupant
options.c: 0.6 inches of clear width per occupant
options.d: 1.0 inch of clear width per occupant

distractorExplanations.a: 0.2 in/person is the factor for level components and ramps, not for stairs.
distractorExplanations.c: 0.6 in/person applies to stairs in health care occupancies, not the general stair factor.
distractorExplanations.d: 1.0 in/person is not an NFPA 101 egress factor; standard stairs use 0.3 in/person.

options.a: Equal at least one-half of the occupant load served
options.b: Equal the occupant load of the largest single room served
options.c: Equal or exceed the total occupant load served
options.d: Exceed the occupant load by a 20 percent safety margin

distractorExplanations.a: The 50% figure is the loss-of-one-means rule for each exit's share, not the total combined capacity.
distractorExplanations.b: Combined capacity must cover all occupants assigned to those exits, not just the largest room's load.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 101 requires capacity at least equal to the load; it does not add a fixed 20% margin.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: All required exits must be sized so aggregate capacity meets or exceeds the occupant load assigned to them. Each component is also sized per code minimums.

options.a: 10 seconds upon loss of normal power
options.b: 30 minutes upon loss of normal power
options.c: 60 minutes upon loss of normal power
options.d: 90 minutes upon loss of normal power

distractorExplanations.a: 10 seconds is the maximum time for emergency lighting to come on, not its required duration.
distractorExplanations.b: 30 minutes is not the NFPA 101 duration; emergency illumination must last at least 1.5 hours.
distractorExplanations.c: 60 minutes falls short of the NFPA 101 requirement of 1.5 hours (90 minutes).

options.a: The fire code for operation and maintenance of existing buildings
options.b: A comprehensive building construction and safety code
options.c: The life safety code governing egress for new and existing buildings
options.d: The standard for installation of sprinkler systems in buildings

distractorExplanations.a: Ongoing fire prevention and maintenance is NFPA 1, Fire Code, not NFPA 5000.
distractorExplanations.c: Egress and occupant life safety are the scope of NFPA 101; NFPA 5000 is the building code.
distractorExplanations.d: Sprinkler installation is NFPA 13; NFPA 5000 references it but is a building construction code.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: NFPA 5000 is NFPA's building construction and safety code, parallel in scope to model codes like the IBC. It covers structural, fire, and life safety provisions.

options.a: Set means of egress design for new and existing buildings
options.b: Establish building construction types and allowable heights
options.c: Provide ongoing fire prevention and operational requirements
options.d: Prescribe inspection and testing of water-based fire protection

distractorExplanations.a: Egress design is NFPA 101's core scope; NFPA 1 extracts it but focuses on fire prevention and operations.
distractorExplanations.b: Construction types and height/area limits are building code (NFPA 5000 or IBC) provisions.
distractorExplanations.d: ITM of sprinklers, standpipes and pumps is NFPA 25; NFPA 1 references it rather than defining it.

options.a: It is more than 25 feet (7.6 m) above the lowest level of fire department access
options.b: It is more than 55 feet (17 m) above the lowest level of fire department access
options.c: It is more than 65 feet (20 m) above the lowest level of fire department access
options.d: It is more than 75 feet (23 m) above the lowest level of fire department access

distractorExplanations.a: 25 ft is not the high-rise threshold; NFPA 101 uses more than 75 ft (23 m) to the highest occupiable floor.
distractorExplanations.b: 55 ft (17 m) is not the high-rise trigger; NFPA 101 defines high-rise at more than 75 ft (23 m).
distractorExplanations.c: 65 ft understates the threshold; NFPA 101 high-rise begins above 75 ft (23 m) to the highest occupiable floor.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: The 75-foot threshold to the lowest fire department access level defines high-rise buildings in NFPA 101. The height is measured to the floor of the highest occupiable story from the lowest level of fire department vehicle access.

options.a: Smokeproof enclosures or pressurized stairs
options.b: Scissor stairs counted as two separate required exits
options.c: Fire escape stairs on the exterior of upper floors
options.d: Increased stair width of 56 inches on all floors

distractorExplanations.b: Scissor stairs address exit count and remoteness when separated; they provide no smoke protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Fire escapes are permitted only for some existing buildings and do not provide high-rise smoke protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Wider stairs add capacity but do not protect against smoke migration into the vertical exit.

options.a: Fire-rated walls with smoke detectors at each stair door
options.b: An open exterior balcony/vestibule or pressurization
options.c: Automatic sprinklers inside the stair at every landing
options.d: A natural vent at the top of the stair shaft

distractorExplanations.a: Rated walls and detection help, but a smokeproof enclosure needs a vestibule or pressurization to keep smoke out.
distractorExplanations.c: Stair sprinklers control fire but do not keep smoke from entering the enclosure.
distractorExplanations.d: A top vent alone can draw smoke into the stair; smokeproof enclosures rely on vestibules or pressurization.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Smokeproof enclosures use vestibules, pressurization, or other approved methods to limit smoke entry into stairs. Fire-rated separation from the building interior is also part of the enclosure.

options.a: Exhaust smoke that enters the stair through a roof-level fan
options.b: Hold a negative pressure in the stair relative to the fire floor
options.c: Maintain a positive pressure differential relative to adjacent spaces
options.d: Equalize pressure so stair doors open with minimal force

distractorExplanations.a: Stair systems pressurize to keep smoke out; exhausting smoke that has entered is a different, weaker approach.
distractorExplanations.b: Negative pressure would draw smoke into the stair, the opposite of pressurization's purpose.
distractorExplanations.d: Equal pressure gives no smoke resistance; the design keeps a differential while limiting door-opening force.

options.a: Replace sprinkler protection in high atrium ceilings
options.b: Pressurize the atrium to keep smoke on the fire floor
options.c: Dilute smoke to below detection levels on all floors
options.d: Manage smoke accumulation in large volume spaces

distractorExplanations.a: Smoke control works with sprinklers; it does not replace them, even at tall ceilings.
distractorExplanations.b: Atrium systems exhaust and manage the smoke layer; pressurization is a stair or zoned smoke-control method.
distractorExplanations.c: Dilution to undetectable levels is not the design goal; the goal is keeping the smoke layer above occupants.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Atrium smoke management uses mechanical exhaust, make-up air, or other engineered methods to control smoke layer development. The goal is tenable conditions for egress and firefighting.

options.a: Calculation of smoke production, exhaust capacity, and make-up air distribution
options.b: A fixed six air changes per hour exhaust rate for the atrium
options.c: Calculation of sprinkler density and hose stream demand for the atrium floor area
options.d: Calculation of stair pressure differentials and door-opening forces at each level

distractorExplanations.b: Air-change rules are not used for atrium design; exhaust is calculated from smoke production and layer height (NFPA 92).
distractorExplanations.c: Sprinkler hydraulics are NFPA 13 calculations; atrium smoke control requires NFPA 92 smoke-filling analysis.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressure differential and door force are stair pressurization checks, not atrium smoke-layer design.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Engineering analysis determines exhaust rates and system response to keep smoke above occupant egress paths for a defined period. Smoke layer interface height is part of the same analysis.

options.a: Visible and audible alarms, with assisted evacuation planned by staff
options.b: An accessible route to exits including ramps, elevators, or areas of refuge
options.c: A dedicated freight elevator reserved for occupants with disabilities during alarms
options.d: Wider exit doors on the ground floor, with upper floors excluded

distractorExplanations.a: Notification and staff plans do not replace a required accessible route to an exit or area of refuge.
distractorExplanations.c: Freight elevators are not an accessible egress element; elevators must meet standby power and lobby requirements.
distractorExplanations.d: Accessible egress must serve each accessible floor, not only the level of exit discharge.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Accessible egress routes must be provided where required, often including elevators with standby power or areas of refuge in certain buildings. Elevators count where permitted, and horizontal exits may be used as allowed.

options.a: A protected space where all occupants of a floor shelter in place during a fire
options.b: A rated room for the fire command center and building controls
options.c: A temporarily tenable space where occupants can await assisted evacuation
options.d: A rated vestibule that keeps smoke out of the adjoining stair enclosure

distractorExplanations.a: Areas of refuge serve occupants unable to use stairs while awaiting help, not whole-floor shelter-in-place.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes the fire command center, which serves firefighters, not occupants awaiting evacuation.
distractorExplanations.d: A vestibule protecting the stair is part of a smokeproof enclosure, not an area of refuge by definition.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Areas of refuge have fire-resistance, communication, and signage so mobility-impaired occupants can safely await rescue. It serves occupants on a floor who cannot use stairs.

options.a: Stay open on magnetic holders that release only by manual action
options.b: Have closers removed where they hinder accessible door operation
options.c: Carry a rating at least equal to the rating of the wall they serve
options.d: Be self-closing or automatic-closing and latch reliably

distractorExplanations.a: Hold-open devices must release on alarm or smoke detection so the door closes without human action.
distractorExplanations.b: Closers cannot be removed from fire doors; opening force is managed with low-energy or power-assisted operators.
distractorExplanations.c: Door ratings are typically lower than the wall (a 90-minute door in a 2-hour wall); equal rating is not required.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Egress fire doors must close to maintain compartmentation; hold-open devices require release upon alarm. The door must maintain the fire-protection rating of the wall assembly.

options.a: The door assembly was tested for that duration in a standard fire test
options.b: The wall in which it is installed must also be rated 90 minutes
options.c: The door also limits unexposed-side temperature rise for 90 minutes
options.d: The door was tested with the building's sprinklers in operation

distractorExplanations.b: A 90-minute door is typically installed in a 2-hour wall; door ratings are usually below the wall rating.
distractorExplanations.c: Temperature-rise performance is a separate label marking, not something the 90-minute rating indicates.
distractorExplanations.d: Fire door tests (UL 10C / NFPA 252) are run without sprinklers; the rating reflects the assembly alone.

options.a: Ducts serving the stair are protected with fire dampers at each floor penetration
options.b: Ducts and piping do not penetrate egress enclosures without proper firestopping
options.c: Sprinkler and electrical lines in stairs use noncombustible pipe and conduit only
options.d: Unrated shafts share the stair enclosure wall to save floor space

distractorExplanations.a: Penetrations not serving the stair are prohibited; dampers do not legitimize general ductwork through exit enclosures.
distractorExplanations.c: Noncombustible pipe still needs listed firestopping; material alone does not maintain the enclosure rating.
distractorExplanations.d: Building service shafts need their own rated enclosure; sharing walls without rating compromises the exit.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Penetrations of fire-rated egress elements require listed firestop systems and code-compliant details to maintain separation. Cabling penetrations need the same listed firestopping and approved details.

options.a: Supply and return fans continue running to dilute smoke on all floors
options.b: Smoke detectors in ducts sound the general evacuation alarm
options.c: Fan shutdown, damper closure, or pressurization sequences are coordinated
options.d: Outside air dampers open fully whenever the building is unoccupied

distractorExplanations.a: Running fans during a fire spreads smoke; NFPA 90A requires shutdown or smoke-control mode on detection.
distractorExplanations.b: NFPA 72 duct detectors typically initiate supervisory signals and fan shutdown, not general evacuation alarms.
distractorExplanations.d: Economizer or night-purge settings are energy controls, not smoke-control sequences tied to egress protection.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Integrated sequences prevent smoke migration and support stair pressurization and zone smoke control strategies. The sequences are coordinated with the fire alarm and stair protection.

options.a: No point in the exit access corridor is more than 50 feet from the nearest sign
options.b: No point in the exit access corridor is more than 75 feet from the nearest sign
options.c: Each exit door has a sign, with directional signs optional in corridors
options.d: No point in the exit access corridor is more than 100 feet from the nearest sign

distractorExplanations.a: 50 ft is not the NFPA 101 limit; signs are placed so no point is more than 100 ft (or the listed viewing distance) away.
distractorExplanations.b: 75 ft is the high-rise height threshold, not the exit sign spacing distance; the limit is 100 ft.
distractorExplanations.c: Directional signs are required wherever the exit or the path to it is not immediately visible to occupants.

options.a: Supplement low-level path marking, especially in high-rise stairs
options.b: Replace emergency lighting along stairs in new high-rise buildings
options.c: Identify fire department connections on building exteriors
options.d: Mark the location of fire extinguishers in assembly spaces

distractorExplanations.b: Photoluminescent markings supplement but do not replace the required 90-minute emergency illumination.
distractorExplanations.c: FDC signage is a separate fire department access marking, not egress path marking.
distractorExplanations.d: Extinguisher location signs are NFPA 10 markings; photoluminescent egress marking outlines the exit path.

options.a: They reduce the clear width available for exit capacity calculations
options.b: They force occupants toward a single direction without an alternative path
options.c: They prevent fire doors from closing at corridor intersections
options.d: They block fire department hose lines from reaching the stair

distractorExplanations.a: Dead ends do not reduce width; the concern is occupants trapped with no alternative route.
distractorExplanations.c: Door operation is unrelated; the limit exists because a dead end offers no second way out.
distractorExplanations.d: Hose deployment is not why NFPA 101 limits dead ends; occupant entrapment is.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: NFPA 101 limits dead-end length so occupants quickly reach a point with egress choice. That risk is greatest if the single path is blocked.

options.a: Moving occupants down an enclosed stair to the level of exit discharge
options.b: Moving occupants along a rated corridor to the nearest exit stair
options.c: Moving occupants through a rated separation into a refuge area on the same floor
options.d: Moving occupants through a smoke barrier into an adjacent smoke compartment on the floor

distractorExplanations.a: Vertical travel through a stair is an interior exit stair, not a horizontal exit.
distractorExplanations.b: A rated corridor is exit access; a horizontal exit is passage through a rated wall to a refuge on the same floor.
distractorExplanations.d: Smoke barriers create smoke compartments; a horizontal exit requires a 2-hour fire barrier and counts as an exit.

options.a: Two exits be at least 30 feet apart, measured along the connecting corridor
options.b: Two exits discharge onto different streets at the public way
options.c: Two exits be separated by at least one-quarter of the overall diagonal
options.d: Two exits be separated so a single fire event is unlikely to block both

distractorExplanations.a: Remoteness uses one-half (or one-third if sprinklered) of the diagonal, not a fixed 30 ft.
distractorExplanations.b: Remoteness applies to exit access and exit separation, not to which street the discharge reaches.
distractorExplanations.c: The diagonal rule is one-half (one-third in sprinklered buildings), not one-quarter.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Exit separation reduces common-mode failure; diagonal or intervening wall separation achieves remoteness. Separation may be by distance or intervening construction.

options.a: Tabulated gross-area factors, with a denser factor for street-floor sales areas
options.b: Net-area factors, with merchandise display fixture areas excluded from the area
options.c: The business occupancy factor of 150 square feet per person gross
options.d: The storage factor of 300 square feet per person gross applied to all sales floors

distractorExplanations.b: Mercantile sales areas use gross area; display fixtures are not deducted from the occupant load calculation.
distractorExplanations.c: 150 sq ft gross is the business-use factor; mercantile sales floors use denser tabulated factors.
distractorExplanations.d: 300 sq ft gross applies to storage, receiving and shipping areas, not to mercantile sales floors.

options.a: Net floor area divided by the business use occupant load factor
options.b: Gross floor area divided by the business use occupant load factor
options.c: The number of workstations shown on the furniture plan
options.d: Gross floor area divided by the assembly occupant load factor

distractorExplanations.a: Business use factors are applied to gross area; net area is used for uses such as classrooms or assembly.
distractorExplanations.c: Furniture plans change; NFPA 101 calculates business occupant load from gross area and the use factor.
distractorExplanations.d: Assembly factors (7 or 15 sq ft net) apply to assembly use, not to general business office space.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Business areas use gross area with the assigned load factor; actual use cannot fall below calculated load for egress design. If the actual occupant count is higher, the higher number is used.

options.a: The calculated load governs, since it is the code's design basis for egress
options.b: The average of the two numbers is used for egress capacity design
options.c: The higher number governs for egress capacity and life safety planning
options.d: The posted certificate of occupancy number governs for that space

distractorExplanations.a: Calculated load is a minimum; NFPA 101 requires the greater actual load to be used when it is higher.
distractorExplanations.b: Averaging understates the real load; the larger of the calculated or actual number governs.
distractorExplanations.d: A posted occupant load may not be exceeded; if actual use is higher, egress must be upgraded for that number.

options.a: To an enclosed interior courtyard open to the sky with no street outlet
options.b: To the ground-floor lobby for every exit stair, with no limit on the number of stairs
options.c: To a rooftop area of refuge accessible by fire department ladders
options.d: Directly to a public way or to an area with unobstructed access to a public way

distractorExplanations.a: A courtyard without a path to the public way is a dead end; discharge must reach a public way.
distractorExplanations.b: NFPA 101 limits interior discharge through the level of exit discharge to 50% of exits under specific conditions.
distractorExplanations.c: Rooftop refuge is not exit discharge; the egress path must end at a public way at grade.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Exit discharge completes the egress path to the public way without locking occupants into enclosed dead ends. Access to the public way must be free as well as unobstructed.

options.a: The occupant load served from the exits discharging into that area
options.b: The clear width of the widest exit door discharging into that area
options.c: The width of the public sidewalk adjacent to the building
options.d: One-half of the occupant load served, since exits discharge in sequence

distractorExplanations.b: Discharge must handle the combined flow from all connected exits, not just match the widest door.
distractorExplanations.c: The sidewalk lies beyond the discharge; discharge components are sized from the occupant load they serve.
distractorExplanations.d: Staggered arrival is not credited; discharge width must accommodate the full load served by connected exits.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Discharge width must accommodate all occupants arriving from connected exits per NFPA 101 capacity calculations. Applicable capacity factors are used for the calculation.

options.a: Sprinklers lower the occupant load factor used for the space
options.b: Sprinklers improve fire control, slowing fire growth
options.c: Sprinklers allow the AHJ to waive emergency lighting requirements
options.d: Sprinklers reclassify the building to a lower hazard of contents

distractorExplanations.a: Sprinklers do not change occupant load factors; they allow travel distance increases in many occupancies.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency lighting is still required in sprinklered buildings; sprinklers do not trade off illumination.
distractorExplanations.d: Hazard of contents classification is based on the materials present, not on sprinkler protection.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Sprinkler trade-ups are occupancy-specific; they reflect improved fire control, not elimination of smoke or exits. This supports safer egress conditions.

options.a: Is an unenclosed corridor that leads occupants to an exit stair
options.b: Requires only smoke-resistant construction instead of a fire rating
options.c: Is a horizontal enclosed component connecting an exit to a public way
options.d: Is a vertical shaft providing access to the roof for firefighters

distractorExplanations.a: An unenclosed corridor leading to a stair is exit access, not an exit passageway.
distractorExplanations.b: Exit passageways need fire barriers matching the exit they serve (1- or 2-hour), not just smoke resistance.
distractorExplanations.d: Vertical roof access is a stair or hatch feature; an exit passageway is a horizontal exit component.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Exit passageways are enclosed, rated corridors that protect horizontal egress between an exit and the public way. It may also be sloped and carries a high fire-resistance rating.

options.a: Corridor leading to an exit stair enclosure
options.b: Door from a room into the exit access corridor
options.c: Aisle within an assembly seating area
options.d: Public way beyond the building property line

distractorExplanations.a: A corridor leading to a stair is a classic exit access element, so it is part of exit access.
distractorExplanations.b: A room door opening to the corridor is part of the exit access path, so it is not the exception.
distractorExplanations.c: Aisles and aisle accessways in assembly seating are exit access elements, so they are not the answer.

options.a: Functional testing at intervals defined by the code, with documentation
options.b: A 30-second test annually, with the 90-minute test every five years
options.c: Visual inspection of lamps quarterly, without a battery discharge test
options.d: Testing only during the annual fire alarm acceptance inspection

distractorExplanations.b: NFPA 101 requires a 30-second test every 30 days and a 1.5-hour test annually, both documented.
distractorExplanations.c: Visual checks miss failed batteries; NFPA 101 requires functional and annual full-duration testing.
distractorExplanations.d: Emergency lighting has its own 30-day and annual test schedule; it is not tied to fire alarm inspections.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Periodic functional and duration testing ensures emergency lighting will perform upon power failure. The AHJ may also set intervals.

options.a: Energize after the fire alarm confirms a fire on the floor
options.b: Energize within 10 seconds of normal power failure
options.c: Energize within 60 seconds of normal power failure
options.d: Energize within 10 minutes of normal power failure

distractorExplanations.a: Emergency lighting responds to loss of normal power, not to fire alarm confirmation of a fire.
distractorExplanations.c: 60 seconds is the Type 60 standby class; egress lighting needs a Type 10 (10-second) source.
distractorExplanations.d: Ten minutes leaves egress paths dark during evacuation; NFPA 101 requires lighting within 10 seconds.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: NFPA 111 and NFPA 101 coordination requires rapid transfer and sustained illumination for egress. It must then sustain the required duration.

options.a: NFPA 5000 governs new construction and NFPA 101 applies to existing buildings alone
options.b: NFPA 101 governs life safety and NFPA 5000 is limited to structural design provisions
options.c: They must be coordinated; conflicts are resolved per local adoption ordinances
options.d: The more recent edition of the two codes governs any conflict

distractorExplanations.a: NFPA 101 applies to new and existing buildings; adopting NFPA 5000 does not limit it to existing ones.
distractorExplanations.b: NFPA 5000 covers construction, fire and life safety, not just structural design, and is coordinated with NFPA 101.
distractorExplanations.d: Edition dates do not resolve conflicts; the adopting ordinance and the codes' own reference rules do.

options.a: Smoke leakage rate measured with a pressure test at each door
options.b: Fire-resistance rating of the wall in which each door is set
options.c: Door width matching the egress capacity calculated for the floor
options.d: Proper closure, latching, labeling, and clearances

distractorExplanations.a: Leakage testing is a listing or acceptance test, not part of NFPA 80 periodic field inspection.
distractorExplanations.b: Wall ratings are verified at plan review; periodic door inspection checks the door assembly's operation.
distractorExplanations.c: Egress width is a design check; fire door inspection verifies closing, latching, labels and clearances.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Fire door inspections focus on operational integrity and maintaining tested assembly performance. Inspectors also look for unapproved field modifications.

options.a: Use fire-rated glazing sized and installed per listing
options.b: Use wired glass of any size in doors rated 90 minutes or less
options.c: Use tempered safety glass sized to the door's impact rating
options.d: Be omitted in doors in 2-hour stair enclosure walls

distractorExplanations.b: Wired glass is limited in size and in hazardous locations; glazing area must match the listing.
distractorExplanations.c: Tempered glass meets impact safety but is not fire-rated; it fails quickly in a fire test.
distractorExplanations.d: Listed vision panels are permitted in 90-minute stair doors within size limits; omission is not required.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Glazing must be part of a listed fire door assembly with size limits per manufacturer listings and NFPA 80. Code limits for the door assembly also apply.

options.a: Close when a fusible link melts at about 165°F
options.b: Close upon detection of smoke to prevent smoke migration
options.c: Open to exhaust smoke from the shaft through the roof
options.d: Close upon manual activation from the fire command center

distractorExplanations.a: Fusible-link closure describes a fire damper; smoke dampers close on smoke detection before heat arrives.
distractorExplanations.c: Dampers protecting egress shafts close to keep smoke out; exhausting through the shaft would pull smoke in.
distractorExplanations.d: Manual override exists for firefighters, but smoke dampers must close on detection without waiting for action.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Damper closure limits smoke spread into stairs and smokeproof enclosures when smoke is detected. This protects vertical egress paths.

options.a: Noncombustible sleeves with the annular space left open for movement
options.b: Fire dampers installed where each pipe passes through the wall
options.c: Listed firestop systems maintaining the enclosure rating
options.d: Mineral wool packing, which is accepted without a listed system

distractorExplanations.a: An open annular space lets fire and smoke pass; the gap must be sealed with a tested firestop system.
distractorExplanations.b: Dampers are for ducts; pipe penetrations are protected by listed firestop systems.
distractorExplanations.d: Mineral wool is a component of many systems but must be installed per a tested, listed firestop design.

options.a: Sending all cars to the fire floor to assist occupant evacuation
options.b: Keeping cars in normal service to speed general evacuation
options.c: Recalling cars once the fire department arrives on scene
options.d: Preventing uncontrolled elevator use during fire

distractorExplanations.a: Phase I recall sends cars to the designated level, away from the fire floor, not toward it.
distractorExplanations.b: Normal elevator use during fire risks stopping at the fire floor; recall removes cars from public service.
distractorExplanations.c: Phase I recall is initiated by lobby, machine room or hoistway detectors, not by fire department arrival.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Phase I/II recall removes elevators from public use during fire, protecting shafts and supporting firefighting. Recall also supports phased evacuation and fire department operations.

options.a: People with disabilities have equivalent access to exits
options.b: Accessible elevators can count toward required exit capacity
options.c: Fewer exits are required in buildings with accessible routes
options.d: Ramps replace stairs as the required exits on upper floors

distractorExplanations.b: Elevators serve as accessible egress where permitted but generally are not counted as required exit capacity.
distractorExplanations.c: Accessible routes do not reduce the number of required exits; exit count depends on occupant load.
distractorExplanations.d: Ramps are not required to replace stairs; accessible egress uses elevators, refuge areas or horizontal exits.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Integrated accessible egress reduces travel distance disparities and avoids unsafe segregated paths. They are not diverted to remote segregated routes.

options.a: Fail locked on power loss to maintain building security
options.b: Have backup operation or manual capability during power failure
options.c: Remain closed until a staff member releases them at a central panel
options.d: Be supplied by the fire alarm panel's standby battery alone

distractorExplanations.a: Fail-secure power doors on egress routes trap occupants; they must open manually or by backup power.
distractorExplanations.c: Staff release adds delay; egress doors must be operable by occupants during a power failure.
distractorExplanations.d: Fire alarm batteries are sized for alarm loads; door operation relies on its own backup or manual capability.

options.a: Be 2-hour fire barriers on every floor level that opens onto the atrium
options.b: Use smoke-resistant construction with no fire-resistance rating needed
options.c: Limit fire and smoke spread while permitting the architectural opening
options.d: Be omitted when the atrium connects no more than six floor levels

distractorExplanations.a: NFPA 101 allows 1-hour separation (or listed glass with sprinklers) and up to three open floors, not 2-hour barriers.
distractorExplanations.b: Atrium separations generally need a 1-hour fire barrier or approved glass wall protection, not just smoke resistance.
distractorExplanations.d: NFPA 101 allows up to three floors open to the atrium without separation, not six.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Atrium design balances rated separation and protected openings with sprinkler and smoke control engineering. The opening arrangement relies on engineered controls.

options.a: High near the ceiling so it pushes smoke toward the exhaust fans
options.b: At 150% of the exhaust volume to pressurize the atrium
options.c: At high velocity near occupants to clear smoke from egress paths
options.d: Low and distributed to avoid disturbing the smoke layer

distractorExplanations.a: High supply mixes into the smoke layer and pushes it down; make-up air must enter below the layer.
distractorExplanations.b: Make-up air is typically less than exhaust (about 85 to 95%) so the atrium stays slightly negative.
distractorExplanations.c: Make-up air velocity is limited (about 200 fpm) so it does not deflect plumes or disturb the smoke layer.

cfps-readiness-check-safety-built-enviro.explanation: Proper make-up air location and volume maintain stratification and prevent smoke layer descent onto occupants. It supplies replacement air for the exhaust volume.

options.a: Door opening force tests and differential pressure measurements
options.b: Air balance of supply registers to match HVAC comfort settings
options.c: Smoke detector sensitivity tests in each stair landing
options.d: Fire damper drop tests in the building's return air ducts

distractorExplanations.b: Comfort air balance is an HVAC task; pressurization commissioning measures pressure differentials and door forces.
distractorExplanations.c: Detector sensitivity is NFPA 72 testing; stair pressurization commissioning verifies pressures and door forces.
